# Accuracy

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/accuracy

# Accuracy

Every result carries a validation report, a short and fixed summary of the checks it passed, with its tier: a
check within the accuracy goal (a relative error of \(10^{-6}\)) is silent; above the goal, within the ceiling (\(10^{-4}\)) or
within the hard limit (\(10^{-2}\)), the result is returned with a warning in the package’s log and as an
AccuracyWarning (Python’s standard filter silences or escalates it), and the flag stays with the result and with
everything computed from it; beyond the hard limit the result is refused.

The numerical settings come in two tested tiers, both held to these checks by the test suite:

```
pp.Settings()            # the default tier
pp.Settings(quick=True)  # a faster tier for exploration

```

The runtime options that set how the package runs (verbosity, timing, cores, platform) change no number; they are on
Runtime options.

Flags and refusals


---

# Velocity anisotropy

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/anisotropy

# Velocity anisotropy

pianistpy.Anisotropy, pianistpy.Component

One class covers every analytical anisotropy model of Chiang+(2026d), Anisotropy(beta_c, r_a, kind):

the default, Anisotropy(), is isotropy;

a finite beta_c alone, in (-infinity, 1), gives constant anisotropy;

a finite anisotropy radius r_a gives the Osipkov-Merritt model (with beta_c = 0) or the
Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) model (with beta_c given), radially biased with kind="I" or tangentially
biased with kind="II".

The comparison at the interface is exact: beta_c=0.0 is isotropic, beta_c=1e-12 is a constant-anisotropy
model, and the object reports which model it is. The general path is continuous through every special value, so
a model a hair away from one agrees with the model at it to the accuracy the tier states.

```
pp.Anisotropy()                           # isotropic
pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)                # constant anisotropy
pp.Anisotropy(r_a=10.0, kind="I")         # Osipkov-Merritt, radially biased
pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=-0.25, r_a=10.0)     # COM, Type I by default

```

Component(profile, anisotropy) joins a density profile and an anisotropy into the input of the inversion.
The first release covers one component per model; several components in one potential are the planned next
extension (Upcoming features).


---

# Line-of-sight velocity distribution in an aperture

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/aperture_losvd

# Line-of-sight velocity distribution in an aperture

pianistpy.aperture_losvd(), pianistpy.Aperture, pianistpy.LosTable

aperture_losvd(source, aperture, v) returns the line-of-sight velocity distribution of the tracers inside an
aperture: the distribution at each projected radius (Line-of-sight velocity distribution) averaged over the aperture with the surface
density,

\[\overline{D}(V_{\rm los}) = \frac{\int_{\rm aperture} \Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})\, D(R_{\rm 2D}, V_{\rm los})\,{\rm d}A}
{\int_{\rm aperture} \Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})\,{\rm d}A}.\]

It is even in \(V_{\rm los}\), integrates to one over all \(V_{\rm los}\), and is zero beyond the escape
velocity along the line of sight. Its second moment is the dispersion inside the aperture,
\(\overline{\sigma}_{\rm los}^2\) (pianistpy.sigma_los_aperture() given the same table).

## Arguments and units

source is a Model or its prepared LosTable; given a model, its table
is built first, so for more than one call build the table once (The prepared table). aperture is an
Aperture, circular or rectangular, centered or offset (Observables), its lengths in the
model’s unit of length. v is an array of line-of-sight velocities in the model’s unit of velocity (km/s in the
physical system); the result has its shape, per unit velocity of the model’s unit system.

Of a superposition, each component’s distribution in the aperture is summed with its weight times its projected
mass inside the aperture, \(\overline{D} = \sum_k w_k M_k \overline{D}_k / \sum_k w_k M_k\).

## Tiers

The distribution is computed on panels in velocity, refined until its norm and its second moment agree with the
table’s rows, and at any velocity it is read by each panel’s polynomial through its own nodes. Its second moment is
checked against the aperture’s dispersion from the projected tables, which reads no velocity distribution, so the
tier is the worse of that check and the table’s own (The prepared table); a distribution above the goal says so in a
warning.

A small aperture costs the quick tier the most. Measured on an NFW halo of concentration 30 with a Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) Type I
anisotropy (\(\beta_{\rm c} = -0.25\), \(R_{\rm a} = 10\)) in a centered circle of radius 0.05 in the scale radius, the
quick tier’s second moment differs from the default tier’s by \(6.7 \times 10^{-6}\) of it, and its own check reports \(6.2 \times 10^{-6}\) (above
the goal, with a warning); in a circle of radius 1 the two differ by \(1.5 \times 10^{-6}\). At the default tier the check reports
\(1.0 \times 10^{-7}\) and \(6.4 \times 10^{-8}\). The quick tier’s table took a quarter of the default’s time.

## Example

```
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
table = pp.LosTable(model)
circle = pp.Aperture.circle(r_ape=1.0)

v = np.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 3001)
d = pp.aperture_losvd(table, circle, v)       # shape (3001,)
dv = v[1] - v[0]
d.sum() * dv                                   # one, to the grid's rule
np.sqrt((v**2 * d).sum() * dv), pp.sigma_los_aperture(table, circle)

pp.aperture_losvd(table, pp.Aperture.circle(r_ape=1.0, r_off=10.0), v)   # an offset circle

```

     On this page

# Distribution functions

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/df

# Distribution functions

pianistpy.compute_df(), pianistpy.DistributionFunction

compute_df(component) returns the untruncated distribution function of a component, from the analytic
inversion of its density, as a DistributionFunction. This is a mathematical object: it is
returned whether or not it is everywhere non-negative and monotonic, and it records where it is not, together
with the smallest truncation value above which it is. It is also the base of Method I truncation, so a scan over
truncations of one model reuses one inversion.

```
halo = pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.nfw(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25))
df = pp.compute_df(halo)

```

A distribution function from elsewhere, a fitting function or another code’s output, is validated the same way:
DistributionFunction.from_function(component, f) takes f(k, depth), which returns the DF (not its
logarithm) at an array of energies in internal units and their depths below the center,
\(P_0 - \mathcal{K}\) (depth), as the grid carries it (a fit in the depth near the center reads it there; a function of the
energy alone may ignore it), tabulates it on the energy grid compute_df places for that component
and settings, and continues it beyond the table, signs it and validates it against the density exactly as the
inversion’s own table. The function gives F only, so the table has no derivative column: its slopes are the
spline’s through F, and the report states that its slope column is not judged. The file stores the table, not
the function, and records the function’s name; a value that is not finite is refused, with the first such
energy. Truncation needs the inversion’s rows, which a distribution function from a function does not carry:
truncate refuses it, by name.

```
import numpy as np
from scipy.special import beta

# the isotropic Plummer model's DF in closed form, F = A K^(7/2)
plummer = pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.plummer(), pp.Anisotropy())
amplitude = 3.0 / (4.0 * np.pi * np.sqrt(2.0) * beta(4.5, 1.5))
df = pp.DistributionFunction.from_function(plummer, lambda k, depth: amplitude * k**3.5)

```

What the result holds: the tabulated distribution function on its energy grid with its logarithmic slope, the
asymptotic form at the center and at the outer end (how the function continues beyond the table), the sign
report, the inputs and the settings it was computed from, its validation report and its identity. A result can
be written to a file and read back equal (Input and output).

A distribution function is not yet a model: only a truncated model can be sampled or
projected.


---

# Differentiable observables

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/differentiable

# Differentiable observables

pianistpy.Differentiable

## The object

pp.Differentiable(model) holds a model of one component on a truncated profile (a distribution function inverted
on its parent’s profile, as pianistpy.truncate() makes it) and serves its observables as JAX functions of the
component’s anisotropy, \(\theta = (\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\), passed as theta. Each method takes \(\theta\) first and mirrors the public call of the
same name, traceable and differentiable in \(\theta\):

```
d = pp.Differentiable(model)
d.sigma_r(theta, r)                    # as pp.sigma_r(model at theta, r)
d.sigma_t(theta, r)                    # as pp.sigma_t
d.sigma_los(theta, r_2d)               # as pp.sigma_los
d.sigma_los_aperture(theta, aperture)  # as pp.sigma_los_aperture
d.losvd(theta, r_2d, v)                # as pp.losvd
d.pdf_v(theta, r, v)                   # as pp.pdf_v
d.aperture_losvd(theta, aperture, v)   # as pp.aperture_losvd

```

Everything is in internal units, whatever the model’s unit system: \(\theta\), as the likelihood’s, the radii and apertures
a method reads, and the velocities it returns. d.theta is the model’s own anisotropy.

The families are those of the distribution function’s own rule (End-to-end differentiability): constant anisotropy (\(\beta_{\rm c}\); an
isotropic or constant component’s \(R_{\rm a}\) is held at its own, infinite, value with a zero gradient), Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) Type I
(\(\beta_{\rm c}\) and \(R_{\rm a}\)), Osipkov-Merritt Type I and Type II (\(R_{\rm a}\)). Refused at construction, each with an error that names it:
COM Type II (its interior point at \(P(R_{\rm a})\) moves with both parameters), a superposition or a model of several
components (its components are differentiated through the likelihood), a component that is not spatially finite, and
one not on a truncated profile that carries its parent’s distribution function.

## What a method computes

A method’s value at \(\theta\) is the public call on the model rebuilt at \(\theta\): at the model’s own \(\theta\), the plain call’s
own value, to the byte. Its derivative is the observable’s tangent rows in \(\theta\) on the tables’ own rows, their
placement frozen, as the likelihood’s free components carry it: between two placements the value moves by the tables’
tolerance, which the derivative does not carry. Over an aperture the derivative is the aperture’s integral of the
tangent rows of the squared dispersion, on the plain call’s own nodes and weights (the integral is linear in the
rows). The line-of-sight velocity distribution, the speed distribution and the aperture’s line-of-sight velocity
distribution take theirs through the distribution function’s own derivative (End-to-end differentiability), their placement frozen;
a member whose distribution function that rule refuses is named at construction, and these three methods raise with
it. At a \(\theta\) where the model is refused the value is not a number and its gradient zero. A method is not
differentiable in its radii.

## The cost

The first time a method meets a \(\theta\), the host rebuilds the model there: the distribution function inverted at \(\theta\)
on the component’s truncated profile, then the dispersion profile and the projected table with their tangent rows.
That is the cost of the likelihood’s own rebuild of a free component, about that of the plain call on the model at
\(\theta\). The last eight \(\theta\) are kept, so the value and the gradient at one \(\theta\) share one rebuild.

The derivative of losvd and aperture_losvd costs far more: it goes back through the rows of the line-of-sight
table, whose transpose recomputes each row and differentiates it in \(\theta\), one row after another in the
calling process. On a CPU node of 32 cores (AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5975WX), the derivative of losvd in
\(\beta_{\rm c}\) at one projected radius and 21 velocities, with the quick settings and a smaller table, did not
finish in 2 h of wall-clock time, with 6 to 7 cores in use on average; the derivative of the example below takes 65 s
there. The values of these methods are not affected.

## Example

The derivative of the line-of-sight dispersion at one projected radius in \(\beta_{\rm c}\), by the rule and by a central
difference of the same function:

```
import jax
import numpy as np

import pianistpy as pp

parent = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy()), pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05)
)
model = pp.solve(pp.Component(parent.profile, pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)))
d = pp.Differentiable(model)

rule = float(jax.grad(lambda t: d.sigma_los(t, 0.3))(d.theta)[0])
h = np.array([1e-3, 0.0])
difference = float(d.sigma_los(d.theta + h, 0.3) - d.sigma_los(d.theta - h, 0.3)) / 2e-3
print(rule, difference)

```

The two agree to the difference’s own error; each of the two shifted \(\theta\) is one rebuild.

     On this page

# Input and output

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/files

# Input and output

Every result (a distribution function, a model, a set of particles) is an immutable object that holds what it
was computed from: the inputs, the numerical settings and the version of the code. Its write method stores
it in a single HDF5 file, and pp.read(path) returns an equal object, whatever kind of result the file holds.
Nothing is written unless requested.

A Model is always a valid equilibrium. A request for which none exists raises UnphysicalModelError, and
the exception carries the distribution function for inspection.


---

# End-to-end differentiability

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/gradient

# End-to-end differentiability

pianistpy.inference.likelihood(), pianistpy.df.gradient.make_inversion_table(),
pianistpy.df.gradient.table_jacobian(), pianistpy.df.gradient.make_inversion_rows(),
pianistpy.df.gradient.rows_jacobian()

## What is differentiable

The weights and the unit scales. The likelihood of a model against data, pianistpy.inference.likelihood(),
is a JAX function of the components’ weights and of the model’s mass and length scales, traceable and differentiable
in both. With free=, the anisotropy \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) of the components named there is a parameter of it as well, for
a component on a truncated profile with a finite \(R_{\rm a}\); the inference page states how.
The two calls serve different members: the rule below serves an untruncated analytic component, while likelihood
refuses a member in free= that is not spatially finite, by name, since it reads the distribution function at
the model’s edge.

The observables. pianistpy.Differentiable serves a model’s observables as JAX functions of its
anisotropy \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\), each with the public call’s own value and the tangent rows’ derivative: Differentiable observables.

The anisotropy parameters. The distribution function of a component is differentiable in its central anisotropy
\(\beta_{\rm c}\) and its anisotropy radius \(R_{\rm a}\), for the families served:

constant anisotropy (\(\beta_{\rm c}\)),

Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) Type I (\(\beta_{\rm c}\) and \(R_{\rm a}\)),

Osipkov-Merritt Type I and Type II (\(R_{\rm a}\)).

Two levels are offered. The inversion’s rows (the distribution function on the inversion’s energy grid) through
make_inversion_rows and rows_jacobian; the distribution function’s table, as the lookup reads it, through
make_inversion_table and table_jacobian. The table’s derivative covers every part of it: the rows, the nodes
below the written floor, the form above the anchor at the center and the tail at the outer end. On a component on
the truncated profile of another model (Method II), the table’s parts are the rows, the edge law below the floor and
the center’s stated form; the rows’ functions serve a component on its own analytic profile only.

make_inversion_rows and make_inversion_table return a JAX function of the parameter vector with a custom
derivative: its value is the package’s own solve, computed on the host, and its derivative is the rule. The
*_jacobian functions return the values and their derivatives as arrays. In both, the energy grid and every
discrete choice of the solve (the grid’s placement, the inversion’s form, the anchor, the nodes kept) are held at the
parameters the function was made at: the derivative is that of the solve with these choices fixed, which is the
derivative of the table the package returns there. Where a choice changes between two parameters, the solve at the
second one differs from the held one by its own tolerance.

Not served, each refused with an error that names it: COM Type II, a center on its critical branch (where
the branch itself changes with \(\beta_{\rm c}\)), and a component on a truncated profile that carries no distribution function
of its model.

COM Type II. The inversion’s kernel carries the factor \((P - P(R_{\rm a}))^s\), with \(s = 1 - \beta_{\rm c} - j\) and \(j\) the
inversion’s order: its interior point \(P(R_{\rm a})\) moves with \(R_{\rm a}\) and its exponent with \(\beta_{\rm c}\). The derivative of that
factor in \(R_{\rm a}\) is not integrable at the interior point for \(s \le 0\), so the rows of the mixed derivative do not
carry the derivative there, and the rule refuses the family for both parameters, naming the interior point. A COM
Type II model’s second moments take their derivative by the Jeans path (dispersion_profile’s tangents); its
distribution function, and the observables read from it (losvd, aperture_losvd, pdf_v), take none.

Where a model’s anisotropy is a parameter. The derivative of a model’s observables in \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\), through
likelihood with free= and through pp.Differentiable, is the full derivative for a Method II model: a
component whose distribution function is inverted on another model’s truncated profile, held fixed, so its profile
and its potential do not move with the anisotropy. A Method I truncated model is refused by name: its truncated
profile is that of its own distribution function, which moves with \(\beta_{\rm c}\) and \(R_{\rm a}\), so neither the Jeans path (a fixed
profile) nor the distribution function’s path at a fixed potential carries the full derivative, and the profile’s
own motion through the truncation is not served in this version. An untruncated model is refused on both paths,
since its edge terms read its distribution function.

On a GPU, the derivative of losvd and aperture_losvd through pp.Differentiable may refuse a row of
the line-of-sight table by name (a ResultError: the row recomputed level by level is not the row): its transpose
recomputes each row and holds it to the forward’s row bit for bit, which a GPU’s order of summation does not
promise. It never returns a wrong number. On the CPU every row is served.

## Per call

pianistpy.inference.likelihood: differentiable in the weights, the unit scales and, with free=, the
\((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) of the named components; the families and refusals as above.

The distribution function (make_inversion_rows, make_inversion_table): differentiable in \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\)
for the families served.

Each observable is differentiable in \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) through pp.Differentiable(model), whose methods mirror the
public calls as JAX functions of \(\theta\), for the families above and with the same refusals.

sigma_r: differentiable in \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) through pp.Differentiable.

sigma_t: differentiable in \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) through pp.Differentiable.

sigma_los: differentiable in \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) through pp.Differentiable.

sigma_los_aperture: differentiable in \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) through pp.Differentiable.

losvd: differentiable in \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) through pp.Differentiable.

aperture_losvd: differentiable in \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) through pp.Differentiable.

pdf_v: differentiable in \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) through pp.Differentiable.

## What the record carries

The rule is exact except for one part, the derivative of the inversion’s operator itself in \(\beta_{\rm c}\) at a fixed
source, which has no closed form and is taken from the operator’s values at nearby \(\beta_{\rm c}\). The record returned with
the derivative states how:

central (a Richardson quotient) inside a form’s region, or one-sided at a corner, where the inversion’s form
changes on one side (integer and half-integer \(\beta_{\rm c}\));

the step, set by measurement: the kernel’s accuracy balanced against the quotient’s truncation term;

the quotient’s Richardson residual and, at a corner, the spread of its two sides, both over the column’s scale;

for a component on a truncated profile, where its energy grid is placed.

The residual is the derivative’s accuracy, and it reads in the package’s tiers (Accuracy). Inside a form’s
region it is at the goal. At the isotropic corner, \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0\), the quotient is one-sided, and its residual is about
\(10^{-5}\) of the column: the ceiling tier, not the goal, which the record states. A gradient there is usable at that
accuracy; one at the goal takes a \(\beta_{\rm c}\) off the corner.

## Example

The derivative of \(\log_{10} F\) at one node of a Hernquist component’s table, by the rule and by a central difference of
the same function:

```
import jax
import numpy as np

import pianistpy as pp
from pianistpy.df.gradient import make_inversion_table

halo = pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25))
table, params, values = make_inversion_table(halo, pp.Settings())
node = int(np.searchsorted(values["k"], 0.5))  # the node nearest K = 0.5

def log_df(theta):
    return table(theta)["log_df"][node]

theta = np.array([0.25])  # params == ("beta_c",)
rule = float(jax.grad(log_df)(theta)[0])
h = 1e-3
difference = float(log_df(theta + h) - log_df(theta - h)) / (2 * h)
print(rule, difference)

```

The two agree to the difference’s own error (\(h^2\) times the third derivative). The table is made once; each
call of table solves the inversion again at the new parameters on the held grid.

     On this page

# The prepared table

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/lostable

# The prepared table

pianistpy.LosTable, pianistpy.losvd(), pianistpy.sigma_los(),
pianistpy.sigma_los_aperture(), pianistpy.sigma_r(), pianistpy.sigma_t(), pianistpy.pdf_v()

LosTable(model) computes once what the observables of a model read: the intrinsic dispersion profile
(Radial velocity dispersion), the surface density \(\Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})\) and the line-of-sight dispersion
\(\sigma_{\rm los}(R_{\rm 2D})\) over projected radius, and the table of line-of-sight velocity distributions
\(D(R_{\rm 2D}, V_{\rm los})\) (Line-of-sight velocity distribution) on rows of projected radius from the center outward (where the
rows run, below).
Every observable then takes the table in place of the model and reads from it, so a table is the object to build
when a model is asked for more than one observable, or for one observable many times (a fit, a grid of apertures).

As in Chiang+(2026d), the dispersion inside an aperture is the surface-density weighted average of
\(\sigma_{\rm los}^2\); a centered circle of radius \(R_{\rm ape}\) gives

\[\overline{\sigma}_{\rm los}^2(R_{\rm ape}) =
\frac{\int_0^{R_{\rm ape}} \Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})\,\sigma_{\rm los}^2(R_{\rm 2D})\,R_{\rm 2D}\,{\rm d}R_{\rm 2D}}
{\int_0^{R_{\rm ape}} \Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})\,R_{\rm 2D}\,{\rm d}R_{\rm 2D}},\]

and an offset circle or a rectangle the same average over its own area. Given the model,
sigma_los_aperture() takes this average and reads no velocity distribution; given the table, it
takes the second moment of the aperture’s velocity distribution, the rows of the table averaged over the aperture
with the same weight. The two routes are independent and agree to the accuracy goal. The table’s route costs
more than the model’s (the example below gives the times).

## Arguments and units

LosTable(model) takes a Model of one component or a superposition; a superposition holds
one table per component (parts), each read with its weight. The table is computed in internal units at the
model’s own settings and is not recomputed for another unit system: table.to("physical", ...) returns the
same tables presented in the units of model.to("physical", ...), and the observables read from it take and
return quantities in those units.

The rows are computed by a pool of worker processes, which Python starts by spawning a fresh interpreter. In a
script, build the table (or call losvd() on a model, which builds one) under
if __name__ == "__main__":, as Python’s multiprocessing requires; in a notebook or an interactive session
nothing is needed.

What it holds: model; profile, projected, kept and table, the results of its four stages;
validation, its report; parts, one table per component.

## Where the rows run

The rows end at the first row beyond which less than losvd.outer_mass_share of the model’s total projected
mass lies (the accuracy goal, \(10^{-6}\), by default). Inside, they start at the profile’s innermost row, unless
losvd.innermost_read_radius names the smallest projected radius the table will be read at: the rows then start at
the last row inside the radius whose disk holds the goal times the projected mass inside innermost_read_radius,
and an aperture’s integral starts at that first row. Each row kept is the row the full table holds at its radius. A
read beyond the last row or inside the first, at a point or over an aperture, is refused by name with that row’s
radius and the setting that moves it; an aperture whose disk inside the first row carries more than the goal of its
weight is refused with the smallest centered circle the table serves at the goal. Settings(losvd={"outer_mass_share":
0}) keeps the rows to the model’s edge.

## Tiers

The rows of the table are added until the table reads itself between rows within the tolerance of its settings,
and every row is checked against two quantities computed without it. The report table.validation holds six
checks, each with its relative error and the radius where it is worst: norm, each row’s integral against the
surface density; second_moment, each row’s second moment against the projected dispersion; unjudged, a row
with surface density that could not be checked (beyond the hard limit if any); t_converged, a row whose rule
along the line of sight ran out of doublings before its tests passed (beyond the hard limit if any); certificate,
the table’s estimate of its reading between rows; and layer_floor, the error at which the quadrature’s layers
toward the point of zero angular momentum stop converging, nonzero only for an anisotropy between 1/2 and 1 at the
center (below the goal: a floor above it is refused). The report’s tier is the worst of these and of the model’s own; a table
above the goal says so in a warning when it is built (Accuracy), and a table beyond the hard limit (tier “refused”)
is refused unless its settings ask for it (Settings(write_anyway=True)), as an aperture’s distribution is. Intervals of projected radius where the
table could not meet its tolerance are recorded in table.table.r_uncertified, and a request inside one is refused by name.

## Example

```
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
table = pp.LosTable(model)                     # built once
table.validation.tier                          # "goal", "ceiling", "warning" or "refused"
{key: check.error for key, check in table.validation.checks.items()}

circle = pp.Aperture.circle(1.0)
pp.sigma_los_aperture(model, circle), pp.sigma_los_aperture(table, circle)   # the two routes
pp.sigma_los(table, [0.1, 1.0, 10.0])
pp.losvd(table, 1.0, [0.0, 0.5, 1.0])

physical = table.to("physical", concentration=10.0, mass_0=1e9, r_0=500.0)
pp.sigma_los_aperture(physical, pp.Aperture.circle(500.0))                   # km/s, 500 pc circle

```

On this example (one 32-core node, CPU), building the table takes about 4 minutes with the node’s 32 workers (43
minutes with one). With the table built, the circle of radius 1 takes about 30 s by the table’s route with 32
workers (6 s with one), against about 3.5 s for the model’s route, and a second aperture over the same table (the
circle of radius 0.5) about as long again.

     On this page


---

# Line-of-sight velocity distribution

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/losvd

# Line-of-sight velocity distribution

pianistpy.losvd(), pianistpy.LosTable

losvd(source, r_2d, v) returns the line-of-sight velocity distribution \(D(R_{\rm 2D}, V_{\rm los})\) at
projected radii: the probability density of the velocity along the line of sight of the tracers seen at a
projected distance \(R_{\rm 2D}\) from the center. As in Chiang+(2026d), it is the distribution function
integrated over the line of sight and over the two velocity components on the plane of the sky,

\[D(R_{\rm 2D}, V_{\rm los}) = \frac{2}{\Sigma(R_{\rm 2D})} \int_{R_{\rm 2D}}^{R_{\rm t}}
\frac{R\,{\rm d}R}{(R^2 - R_{\rm 2D}^2)^{1/2}} \iint F(\mathcal{Z}, L)\,{\rm d}V_{\perp 1}\,{\rm d}V_{\perp 2},
\qquad
\Sigma(R_{\rm 2D}) = 2 \int_{R_{\rm 2D}}^{R_{\rm t}} \frac{\varrho(R)\,R\,{\rm d}R}{(R^2 - R_{\rm 2D}^2)^{1/2}},\]

with the inner integral over the plane-of-sky velocities at which the truncated distribution function is
positive. It is even in \(V_{\rm los}\), integrates to one over all \(V_{\rm los}\), and is zero beyond the
escape velocity along the line of sight. Its second moment is \(\sigma_{\rm los}^2\) (pianistpy.sigma_los()).

## Arguments and units

source is a Model or its prepared LosTable; given a model, its table
is built first, so for more than one call build the table once (The prepared table, which also says how to call it
from a script). r_2d and v are arrays
that broadcast against each other: projected radii in the model’s unit of length (internal units by default,
parsecs or an Astropy quantity in the physical system) and line-of-sight velocities in its unit of velocity (km/s
in the physical system). The result has their broadcast shape, per unit velocity of the model’s unit system.

Of a superposition, each component’s distribution is read from its own table and the components are summed with
their weights times their surface densities, \(D = \sum_k w_k \Sigma_k D_k / \sum_k w_k \Sigma_k\).

## Tiers

The distribution is read from the rows of the table between rows by the same reading the table checked its rows with,
so the tier is that of the table (The prepared table): each row’s norm against the surface density and its second
moment against the projected dispersion, and the table’s estimate of its reading between rows. A projected radius
in an interval where the table could not meet its tolerance is refused by name.

## Example

```
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
table = pp.LosTable(model)

v = np.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 3001)
d = pp.losvd(table, 1.0, v)                    # at R_2D = 1, shape (3001,)
dv = v[1] - v[0]
d.sum() * dv                                   # one, to the grid's rule
np.sqrt((v**2 * d).sum() * dv), pp.sigma_los(table, 1.0)

pp.losvd(table, np.array([[0.1], [1.0], [10.0]]), v).shape   # (3, 3001): radii by velocities

```

     On this page


---

# Models

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/models

# Models

A model is built in four steps, one page each: a density profile, a velocity anisotropy on it, the distribution
function of that pair, and the truncation in phase space that makes the finite equilibrium.

Density profiles (DoublePowerLaw)

Velocity anisotropy (Anisotropy, Component)

Distribution functions (compute_df)

Truncation in phase space (truncate, solve)


---

# Observables

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/observables

# Observables

pianistpy.sigma_los(), pianistpy.sigma_los_aperture(), pianistpy.aperture_losvd(),
pianistpy.Aperture, pianistpy.LosTable

Observables are functions of a model. A single request computes only what it needs; for repeated requests on one
model, the prepared object LosTable(model) tabulates the line-of-sight velocity distributions once and every
observable reads from it.

```
sigma = pp.sigma_los(model, [0.1, 1.0, 10.0])        # at projected radii

circle = pp.Aperture.circle(r_ape=1.0, r_off=0.0)
slit = pp.Aperture.rectangle(side_x=2.0, side_y=0.2, r_off=0.0, angle=0.0)
pp.sigma_los_aperture(model, circle)                 # averaged over an aperture
pp.sigma_los_aperture(model, slit)

table = pp.LosTable(model)                           # once, for many requests
pp.sigma_los(table, [0.1, 1.0, 10.0])
pp.sigma_los_aperture(table, circle)
pp.aperture_losvd(table, circle, [0.0, 0.1, 0.2])    # the distribution in the aperture

```

An Aperture is circular or rectangular, centered or offset, the rectangle at an angle; every aperture call
takes the same object. The intrinsic radial and tangential dispersions and the line-of-sight velocity
distribution itself are available in the same way; their public names are listed in the
API reference. The distribution’s Gauss-Hermite moments (h3, h4)
enter the inference as data (pianistpy.inference.Data); they are not an observable call of their own.

Pairs of projected radius and line-of-sight velocity are drawn by ProjectedSampler on an annulus and, if
given, in a window of velocity, exactly conditioned: the radius carries the window’s share of the distribution
at each radius, for every anisotropy. The ranges and the pairs are in the source’s unit system, as for the other
observables; the tables it builds carry their errors in its report.

```
from pianistpy.observables import ProjectedSampler

sampler = ProjectedSampler(table, R_range=(0.1, 3.0), v_range=(-0.2, 0.3))
pairs = sampler.sample(1_000_000, seed=1)   # pairs.r_2d, pairs.v_los, pairs.mass

```

An aperture of arbitrary shape is not an exact route: the notebook of the same name shows how a mask on
projected draws gives it, with the statistical error printed beside every number (Examples).

One page per call, each with its definition, its arguments and units, the tiers it reports and an example:

Radial velocity dispersion (sigma_r)

Tangential velocity dispersion (sigma_t)

Line-of-sight velocity distribution (losvd)

Line-of-sight velocity distribution in an aperture (aperture_losvd)

Local speed distribution (pdf_v)

The prepared table (LosTable)

End-to-end differentiability

Differentiable observables (Differentiable)

# Particles

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/particles

# Particles

pianistpy.Sampler, pianistpy.particles.Particles

Sampler(model) prepares the sampling tables of a model once; .sample(n, seed) then returns n
equal-mass particles as a Particles result, with positions, velocities, masses and component labels in
memory. The draw is by inversion, with no rejection step, and is reproducible particle by particle: each
particle is determined by the seed, its component and its index, independently of the hardware and of the
number of particles requested.

```
sampler = pp.Sampler(model)
particles = sampler.sample(10_000_000, seed=1)
particles.write("halo.h5")                     # the native HDF5 layout
particles.write("halo_gamer.bin", layout="gamer")
particles.write("halo_gadget.hdf5", layout="gadget")
particles.write("halo.txt", layout="text")

```

The layouts: the native HDF5 file, read back by pianistpy.read(); the particle file of
GAMER; a Gadget HDF5
initial condition; fixed-width text with the units in its header. Every writer reads its file back and compares
it with what it wrote before returning. A writer for another simulation code is one registered function.

A model that is not spatially finite needs an explicit sampling radius; the sampler holds the mass inside it
(Sampler.radius_table.mass_sample, in internal units).

Sampler(model, r_range=(r_lo, r_hi)) draws every particle between two radii, in internal units, inside the
sampling. The draw is the model’s own conditioned on the range, not a selection after a full draw: each
particle’s radius number is taken between the mass fractions of r_lo and r_hi, so every particle lands in
the range, and the particles carry the range’s mass. A superposition is drawn in the range by its components’
weights, which the range leaves unchanged.

Sampler.speeds(r, seed, v_range=(v_lo, v_hi)) draws one speed at each given radius from the model’s speed
distribution at that radius conditioned on the window, in internal units, and returns with the speeds the fraction
of the distribution at each radius that the window holds. v_lo and v_hi are floats, one window for every
radius, or arrays that broadcast against r, a window at each radius (a grid in units of each radius’s escape
speed is one call per grid speed). Each speed number is taken between the speed table’s own
numbers for v_lo and v_hi, so every speed lands in the window; a window wider than the escape speed draws the
speeds of sample at the same seed. A superposition takes each component by its share of the window. The window is
drawn for a constant anisotropy only: with a finite anisotropy radius the speed carries a factor of the drawn angle,
so the window couples to the angle, and such a model is refused.

## Where the speed table reaches its tier

A model whose distribution function is non-negative is not thereby samplable at every tier. The speed table’s
rows are refined until the error across them is under the goal or their count reaches n_rows_max; the table’s
report carries that error, and a table beyond the hard limit is refused (Accuracy). Close to the smallest
anisotropy radius \(R_{\rm a,min}\) (r_a_min) at which an Osipkov-Merritt or Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) Type I distribution function is
non-negative, the rows reach n_rows_max first and the error grows steeply as \(R_{\rm a}\) falls toward
\(R_{\rm a,min}\). Measured on a truncated NFW density of concentration 10 (truncation radius 31.9 scale radii) at the
default tier, the error crosses the ceiling and the hard limit at:

model

\(\beta_{\rm c}\)

ceiling \(10^{-4}\) at \(R_{\rm a}/R_{\rm a,min}\)

hard limit \(10^{-2}\) at \(R_{\rm a}/R_{\rm a,min}\)

COM I

-0.75

1.62

1.16

COM I

-0.50

1.84

1.20

COM I

-0.25

1.38

1.10

OM I

0

1.27

1.07

COM I

+0.05

1.24

1.07

COM I

+0.25

1.14

1.04

COM I

+0.40

1.09

1.02

COM I

+0.45

above 1.23

1.02

Above the first ratio the table is within the ceiling; between the two it is returned with a warning; below the
second it is refused. At \(\beta_{\rm c} = 1/2\) the distribution function is non-negative at every \(R_{\rm a}\), and the
table is beyond the hard limit at every \(R_{\rm a}\) up to 0.32 scale radii. A constant-anisotropy model is within the
ceiling up to \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0.4\) (row error \(6 \times 10^{-5}\)) and above it at \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0.45\) (\(4 \times 10^{-4}\)). These bounds are
measured, not imposed: each table’s own report is the verdict.

     On this page


---

# Local speed distribution

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/pdf_v

# Local speed distribution

pianistpy.pdf_v(), pianistpy.LosTable

pdf_v(source, r, v) returns the local speed distribution \(p(V\,|\,R)\) at 3D radii: the probability density
of the speed \(V = |\mathbf{V}|\) of the tracers at a distance \(R\) from the center. As in Chiang+(2026d), the
density at a radius is split into the velocity angle \(\varphi\) and the speed,

\[\varrho(R) = 2\pi \int_0^\pi {\rm d}\varphi\; p_\varphi(\varphi\,|\,R)
\int_0^{V_{\rm esc}(R)} {\rm d}V\; p_V(V\,|\,R, \varphi),
\qquad V_{\rm esc}(R) = \sqrt{2P(R)},\]

and the speed distribution is the inner density integrated over the angle, normalized by \(\varrho(R)\):

\[p(V\,|\,R) = \frac{2\pi}{\varrho(R)} \int_0^\pi p_\varphi(\varphi\,|\,R)\, p_V(V\,|\,R, \varphi)\,{\rm d}\varphi .\]

It integrates to one over \(V \geq 0\). Its support ends at the escape speed \(V_{\rm esc}(R)\) for an
isotropic, constant-anisotropy or Type I model; a Type II model holds orbits of negative energy as well, and its
speeds reach \(V_{\rm esc}/\sqrt{1 - R^2/R_{\rm a}^2}\). The radius \(R\) of Chiang+(2026d) is r in the
package.

## Arguments and units

source is a Model or its prepared LosTable, whose intrinsic second
moments the distribution is checked against. r and v are arrays that broadcast against each other: radii
in the model’s unit of length (internal units by default, parsecs or an Astropy quantity in the physical system)
and speeds in its unit of velocity (km/s in the physical system). The result has their broadcast shape, per unit
velocity of the model’s unit system, and is zero at negative speeds and beyond the end of the support.

Of a superposition, the components are mixed by their density at the radius,
\(p = \sum_k w_k \varrho_k p_k / \sum_k w_k \varrho_k\).

## Tiers

Each radius asked for is computed once, with three checks: the norm of the distribution against the density, its
second moment against \(\sigma_{\rm r}^2 (3 - 2\beta_\sigma)\) from Radial velocity dispersion, and the change of the
distribution when the nodes of its angle rule double. The nodes double, at most three times, until that change is
under speed_tolerance (the goal \(10^{-6}\) at the default tier, the ceiling \(10^{-4}\) at the quick tier). A distribution
above the goal is returned with a warning; one beyond the hard limit is refused with an
AccuracyError unless the model’s settings ask for it (write_anyway). The stage behind the
call, pianistpy.observables.stages.speed_distribution(), returns the distribution at one radius with its
record, its escape speed, the end of its support and, for a Type II model, the share of it beyond the escape
speed (unbound_fraction).

## Example

```
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
v = np.linspace(0.0, 1.4, 1401)                           # past the escape speed at every r here
p = pp.pdf_v(model, np.array([[0.1], [1.0], [10.0]]), v)   # (3, 1401): radii by speeds
p.sum(axis=1) * (v[1] - v[0])                              # each about one

physical = model.to("physical", concentration=10.0, mass_0=1e9, r_0=500.0)
pp.pdf_v(physical, 500.0, [10.0, 50.0, 100.0])             # per km/s, at 500 pc

```

     On this page


---

# Density profiles

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/profiles

# Density profiles

pianistpy.DoublePowerLaw

An analytical double-power-law density profile with a finite central potential (an inner slope below 2), in
its three slopes, DoublePowerLaw(rho_alpha, rho_beta, rho_gamma): the inner slope,
the outer slope and the sharpness of the transition between them, with the scale radius and the central
potential of the untruncated profile set to one (the internal units, Units). The named profiles are
presets of the same class, not classes of their own:

```
pp.DoublePowerLaw.nfw()        # Navarro-Frenk-White
pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist()
pp.DoublePowerLaw.plummer()
pp.DoublePowerLaw(1.0, 3.0, 1.0)   # the same NFW profile by its slopes

```

A profile holds its density, enclosed mass and potential as closed forms; every quantity of the package is
computed from them by one path, and the named profiles’ textbook forms are test references only.

A profile is one half of a pianistpy.Component; the other half is its anisotropy.
A component takes an outer slope of 3 or more: between 2 and 3 the outer end of the inversion is not available
in this version, and the component is refused by name (OUTER SLOPE).


---

# Flags and refusals

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/results

# Flags and refusals

What the package returns, what it flags and what it refuses, in one place.

## The distribution function is always returned

compute_df returns the distribution function of any component the inversion defines, whatever its sign. Where
it is negative the result says so, with the zero crossing, the minimum and the smallest truncation value above
which the truncated function is non-negative.

## A model is always a valid equilibrium

truncate and solve return a Model only where one exists. A request for which there is
no physical, stable equilibrium raises UnphysicalModelError; the exception carries the
distribution function, so nothing is lost and nothing has to be recomputed. A Method II request whose anisotropy
is incompatible with the parent’s edge is refused at the call by the existence condition, with the admissible
range stated.

## A model that is not spatially finite is a model

A truncated model whose density does not reach zero at a finite radius, or whose mass does not converge, is
returned with spatially_finite false and its truncation radius and total mass stated as not finite. This is a
property, not an error, and comes with no accuracy warning. What needs finiteness asks for it by name: a
truncation by target mass or target radius has no solution there and is refused with the reachable range;
sampling requires an explicit sampling radius and records the mass inside it; observables state the radius to
which they hold.

## A distribution function that diverges at the truncation energy

A Method II child whose anisotropy is more than one unit below its parent’s has a distribution function that
diverges, integrably, at the truncation energy. It is returned, with a warning that names the exponent and says
the model is a valid equilibrium of finite density whose stability is not established.

## The accuracy tiers

Every result carries a validation report: a short and fixed summary of the checks it passed, one record per
check, with its tier. A check within the accuracy goal (a relative error of \(10^{-6}\)) is silent. Above the goal,
within the ceiling (\(10^{-4}\)) or within the hard limit (\(10^{-2}\)), the result is returned with a warning in the package’s
log and as an AccuracyWarning (Python’s standard filter silences or escalates it), and the
flag stays with the result and with everything computed from it. Beyond the hard limit the result is refused.

## One component

The first release covers one component per model. compute_df and solve refuse more than one; several
components in one potential, and tracers in a fixed potential, are the planned next extension
(Upcoming features).

## The keys to read first in a result

validation (the report and its tier), spatially_finite, r_t and mass_t (the truncation radius
and the total mass), identity (what the result was computed from), units (the system it is presented in),
timing (the wall time of each stage) and, on a file, the backend that made it.

     On this page


---

# Radial velocity dispersion

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_r

# Radial velocity dispersion

pianistpy.sigma_r(), pianistpy.LosTable

sigma_r(source, r) returns the intrinsic radial velocity dispersion \(\sigma_{\rm r}\) at 3D radii: the second
moment of the radial velocity over the model’s distribution function at a fixed radius. As in Chiang+(2026d), it is
the velocity moment of the augmented density \(\varrho_{\rm aug}(P, R)\) taken at the potential of the radius,

\[\sigma_{\rm r}^2(R) = \frac{1}{\varrho_{\rm aug}(P, R)} \int_0^{P} \varrho_{\rm aug}(\mathcal{K}, R)\,
{\rm d}\mathcal{K}, \qquad P = P(R),\]

which for the anisotropy models of the package, whose augmented density separates as
\(\varrho_{\rm aug}(P, R) = \varrho_{\rm aux}(P)\,g(R)\), is the Jeans integral of \(\varrho_{\rm aux}\)
over the potential. The radius \(R\) of Chiang+(2026d) is r in the package.

## Arguments and units

source is a Model (one component, or a superposition) or its prepared
LosTable, which holds the same intrinsic profile. r is an array of radii in the model’s
unit system: internal units by default (the scale radius is 1), parsecs (a float or an Astropy quantity) after
model.to("physical", ...). The result has the shape of r, in the model’s velocity unit (km/s in the
physical system).

Of a superposition, whose components share one density, the second moments add with the weights:
\(\sigma_{\rm r}^2 = \sum_k w_k \sigma_{{\rm r},k}^2\).

## Tiers

The profile is tabulated once per model in radius, with rows added until every interval between rows reads
within profile_tolerance at its midpoint (\(10^{-7}\) at the default tier, \(10^{-6}\) at the quick tier; a tenth of the
goal, the profile’s share of the error of what is projected from it). A model beyond the hard limit is refused
unless its settings ask for it (write_anyway), as for every observable (Accuracy).

## Example

```
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

# a Hernquist density with a constant anisotropy of 0.25, truncated at K_t = 0.05
model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
r = np.array([0.1, 1.0, 10.0])
pp.sigma_r(model, r)                          # internal units

physical = model.to("physical", concentration=10.0, mass_0=1e9, r_0=500.0)
pp.sigma_r(physical, [50.0, 500.0, 5000.0])   # parsecs in, km/s out

```

     On this page


---

# Tangential velocity dispersion

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/sigma_t

# Tangential velocity dispersion

pianistpy.sigma_t(), pianistpy.LosTable

sigma_t(source, r) returns the intrinsic tangential velocity dispersion \(\sigma_{\rm t}\) at 3D radii, of both
tangential components together, \(\sigma_{\rm t}^2 = \sigma_\theta^2 + \sigma_\phi^2\). As in Chiang+(2026d), it is the
tangential velocity moment of the augmented density,

\[\sigma_{\rm t}^2(R) = \frac{2}{\varrho_{\rm aug}(P, R)} \int_0^{P}
\frac{\partial}{\partial R^2}\Big[R^2 \varrho_{\rm aug}(\mathcal{K}, R)\Big]\,{\rm d}\mathcal{K},
\qquad P = P(R),\]

so that the anisotropy is \(\beta_\sigma = 1 - \sigma_{\rm t}^2 / (2\sigma_{\rm r}^2)\): zero for an isotropic model,
\(\beta_{\rm c}\) for a constant anisotropy, and \(R^2 / (R^2 + R_{\rm a}^2)\) for an Osipkov-Merritt
Type I model. The package evaluates it as \(\sigma_{\rm t}^2 = 2(1 - \beta_\sigma)\sigma_{\rm r}^2\), with
\(\sigma_{\rm r}\) from Radial velocity dispersion and \(\beta_\sigma\) from the model’s anisotropy in closed form.

## Arguments and units

As for Radial velocity dispersion: source is a Model or its LosTable, r is in
the model’s unit system, and the result has the shape of r in the model’s velocity unit. Of a superposition,
\(\sigma_{\rm t}^2 = \sum_k w_k \sigma_{{\rm t},k}^2\).

## Tiers

Those of Radial velocity dispersion, whose profile it reads: the anisotropy factor is exact.

## Example

The anisotropy read back from the two dispersions is the model’s own, here constant with
\(\beta_{\rm c} = 0.25\).

```
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp

model = pp.solve(
    pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.hernquist(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25)),
    pp.Truncation(k_t=0.05),
    settings=pp.Settings(quick=True),
)
r = np.array([0.1, 1.0, 10.0])
beta = 1.0 - pp.sigma_t(model, r) ** 2 / (2.0 * pp.sigma_r(model, r) ** 2)
np.max(np.abs(beta - 0.25))   # rounding

```

     On this page


---

# Superposition and inference

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/superposition

# Superposition and inference

pianistpy.superpose(), pianistpy.inference

## Superposition

Distribution functions inverted from one truncated density (Method II children of one parent), combined with
positive weights that sum to one, are one equilibrium model in that density. superpose returns it as a
Model, so everything downstream (particles, observables, files) takes it unchanged.

```
members = {child_a: 0.6, child_b: 0.3, child_c: 0.1}   # Method II children of one parent
composite = pp.superpose(members)
pp.Sampler(composite).sample(1_000_000, seed=1)

```

The shared density is enforced: members on different truncated profiles are refused. The weights are normalized;
a sum away from one is normalized with a warning.

## Inference

pianistpy.inference gives the log-likelihood of a model against data as a JAX function of the
components’ weights and the scales of the units, linear in the weights up to their normalization, so its
gradient with respect to the weights is exact and cheap.

```
from pianistpy.inference import Data, likelihood

data = Data("sigma_los", values=sigma_obs, r_2d=radii, errors=sigma_err, unit_system="physical")
loglike = likelihood(composite.to("physical", concentration=..., mass_0=..., r_0=...), data)
loglike(weights)                       # a JAX scalar; jax.grad(loglike)(weights) is its gradient

```

The members’ observables are computed once, in likelihood; each call of the returned function costs a
fraction of a millisecond. A refused input inside the traced function (negative weights, a radius outside the
table) gives minus infinity, never an exception, so a sampler over the weights sees a value.

What the likelihood is differentiable in, through which observables, and at what accuracy: End-to-end differentiability.

     On this page


---

# Runtime options

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/switches

# Runtime options

None of these changes a number, except the platform: results on a GPU and a CPU agree to better than
\(10^{-10}\) in relative terms, and each file records which made it.

```
pp.set_verbosity("info")   # "quiet" (the default), "info" or "debug"
pp.set_timing(True)        # print the wall time of each stage
pp.set_workers("half")     # "auto" (the default), "full", "half" or a number of cores
pp.set_compilation_cache(False)  # the compilation cache is on by default; a path moves it
pp.set_platform("cpu")     # "auto" (the default), "cpu" (the CPU-only mode) or "gpu"; before the first computation

```

The CPU-only mode gives the same numbers on every machine; the environment variable PIANISTPY_PLATFORM=cpu
sets it before the package is imported. Each file records the backend that made it.

On shared clusters, a GPU in the Exclusive_Process compute mode serves one process at a time; if another process
holds it, JAX stops with Unable to initialize backend 'cuda'. Free the GPU, share it through an MPS daemon
(nvidia-cuda-mps-control -d), or use the CPU-only mode.

The workers’ switch sets how many cores the package’s parallel work uses; "auto" uses every allowed core
inside a batch job and half of them anywhere else, and no value changes a number. The verbosity, the timing and
the workers can also be set by the environment variables PIANISTPY_VERBOSITY, PIANISTPY_TIMING and
PIANISTPY_WORKERS, in any case; PIANISTPY_TIMING reads 1, true, yes or on and 0,
false, no or off, and any other value is refused by name.

The compilation cache keeps JAX’s compiled kernels between sessions in one folder: ~/.cache/pianistpy/jax
by default, or the folder the environment variable PIANISTPY_COMPILATION_CACHE names (off, 0,
false or no turns the cache off). The switch returns the folder in use, and the cache changes no number.


---

# Truncation in phase space

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/truncation

# Truncation in phase space

pianistpy.Truncation, pianistpy.truncate(), pianistpy.solve(), pianistpy.Model

## Method I

truncate(df, truncation) returns a Model: the distribution function truncated at an energy,
with the self-consistent potential-density pair that follows from it. A Model is by construction a physical
and stable equilibrium; a request for which none exists is refused with UnphysicalModelError,
which carries the distribution function for inspection.

One limit is stated rather than solved: for a steep cusp at \(\beta_{\rm c} = -1/2\) the self-consistent center of the
truncated model is not reached (measured on \((\alpha, \beta) = (2, 4)\) at \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t} = 0.3\), from \(\gamma = 1.735\) on), and the call
refuses it with an AccuracyError that names the iteration’s response.

Truncation takes exactly one of three targets:

```
pp.Truncation(k_t=0.2)                          # the truncation energy, in internal units
pp.Truncation(mass_t=1.0, concentration=10.0)   # a target mass, in units of M_0 (model units)
pp.Truncation(r_t=5.0)                          # a target radius, in units of the scale radius

```

A target mass is given in units of \(M_0\), so it needs the concentration that defines \(M_0\); a target radius and a
truncation energy do not, and a concentration given with them is refused.

solve(component, truncation) runs compute_df and truncate at once.

What a model holds: the truncated distribution function, the truncated density, potential and enclosed mass on
one radial grid (model.profile.r, .rho_trunc, .p_trunc, .mass_trunc), the truncation radius and
the total mass, the validation report and the identity. A model that is not spatially finite is still a model:
it says so (spatially_finite is false), states its radius and mass as not finite, and what needs finiteness
asks for it by name (Flags and refusals).

A Type II model (Osipkov-Merritt or Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt) must end inside its anisotropy radius \(R_{\rm a}\), where its density
\(\varrho_{\rm aux} / (1 - R^2/R_{\rm a}^2)\) has a pole. The lower bound \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t} > P(R_{\rm a})\) keeps the untruncated radius of the truncation
energy inside \(R_{\rm a}\), but the truncated model’s own edge lies farther out; where that edge would reach \(R_{\rm a}\) the request
is refused by name (TYPE II EDGE, with the potential at \(R_{\rm a}\) stated), and a larger \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\) brings the edge
inside. The bound is strict, so where it sets a Type II DF’s k_t_min that is the next float above \(P(R_{\rm a})\), the
smallest \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\) the gates admit: necessary, not sufficient, since only the truncated solve places the edge.

An Osipkov-Merritt Type I model with a small \(R_{\rm a}\) and a low \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\) can leave no edge within the solve’s radius;
the request is refused by name (NO EDGE). On the Hernquist density at the quick settings, \(R_{\rm a} = 1\) is refused at
every \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t}\) from 0.005 to 0.3, \(R_{\rm a} = 2\) below \(\mathcal{K}_{\rm t} = 0.2\), \(R_{\rm a} = 5\) below 0.03 and \(R_{\rm a} = 10\) at 0.005; the parents that
build are at the ceiling tier, set by their distribution function’s high_k_slope_mismatch (\(3.4 \times 10^{-6}\), at \(\mathcal{K} = 1\)).

## Method II

Method II gives a new anisotropy to a density that is already truncated: a component whose profile is the
truncated profile of another model, through the same functions.

```
parent = pp.solve(pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.nfw(), pp.Anisotropy()), pp.Truncation(k_t=0.2))
child = pp.solve(pp.Component(parent.profile, pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=-0.25)))

```

A Method II model exists only when its anisotropy is compatible with the edge of the parent’s density; the
condition is checked at the call and a violation is refused by name, with the admissible range stated. The
technical notes derive it (Technical notes).

     On this page


---

# Units

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/guide/units

# Units

Everything is computed in internal units, the dimensionless normalization of Widrow (2000) in which the scale
radius and the central potential of the untruncated profile are 1. The to method of a model (and of a
line-of-sight table) presents it in model units (\(G = M_0 = r_0 = 1\)) or, through
Astropy, in physical units, without recomputing it, and what is computed from it
(the observables, the particles) is returned in that system.
The ranges of a draw are the exception: Sampler’s r_range and the v_range of Sampler.speeds are
given in internal units.

Three inputs of a truncation are given in the units that are natural for them, as their documentation states:
the truncation energy k_t in internal units, a target radius r_t in units of the scale radius, and a
target mass mass_t in units of \(M_0\), together with the concentration that defines \(M_0\).


---

manual renders them and runs nothing. The notebooks live in their own repository,
PIANISTpy-notebooks, from which they can be opened in

# Compute observables from a model

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/notebooks/tutorials/observables

# Compute observables from a model

The line-of-sight velocity dispersion at projected radii, its average over an aperture, and the same quantities in physical units. This tutorial uses the isotropic Hernquist model, whose distribution function is known in closed form.

```
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp
from pianistpy.df.analytic import analytic_model

model = analytic_model("hernquist")

```

sigma_los takes projected radii, in the model’s units (internal here: the scale radius is 1).

```
r_2d = np.array([0.1, 1.0, 10.0])
pp.sigma_los(model, r_2d)

```

```
array([0.30974035, 0.27598987, 0.1234161 ])

```

sigma_los_aperture averages the squared dispersion over an aperture, weighted by the surface density: a centered circle, or a rectangle at an offset and an angle.

```
circle = pp.Aperture.circle(1.0)
slit = pp.Aperture.rectangle(2.0, 0.5, r_off=1.0, angle=0.3)
pp.sigma_los_aperture(model, circle), pp.sigma_los_aperture(model, slit)

```

```
(0.3028872393345692, 0.3003436495218896)

```

A LosTable computes the line-of-sight velocity distributions once and serves every call made from it. Its aperture dispersion is the second moment of the aperture’s velocity distribution, an independent route that agrees with the one from the model.

```
table = pp.LosTable(model)
pp.sigma_los(table, r_2d), pp.sigma_los_aperture(table, circle)

```

```
(array([0.30974035, 0.27598987, 0.1234161 ]), 0.302887239623593)

```

In physical units, radii and apertures are given in parsecs (or as Astropy quantities) and the dispersions are returned in km/s. Here \(M_0 = 10^9\) solar masses and \(r_0 = 500\) pc, with a concentration of 10.

```
physical = model.to("physical", concentration=10.0, mass_0=1e9, r_0=500.0)
pp.sigma_los(physical, [50.0, 500.0, 5000.0])

```

\[[31.599922,~28.156675,~12.590995] \; \mathrm{\frac{km}{s}}\]

```
pp.sigma_los_aperture(
    table.to("physical", concentration=10.0, mass_0=1e9, r_0=500.0), pp.Aperture.circle(500.0)
)

```

\[30.900763 \; \mathrm{\frac{km}{s}}\]


---

# Generate particle initial conditions

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/notebooks/tutorials/particles

# Generate particle initial conditions

A Sampler holds the tables that drawing particles needs; it is built once from a Model and reused by every call of sample. This tutorial draws particles from the isotropic Hernquist model, whose distribution function is known in closed form, so that it runs without the inversion.

```
import numpy as np
import pianistpy as pp
from pianistpy.df.analytic import analytic_model

model = analytic_model("hernquist")
model.spatially_finite, model.validation.tier

```

```
(False, 'goal')

```

The Hernquist model is not truncated, so the sampler needs an outer radius, r_sample, in internal units (the scale radius is 1).

```
sampler = pp.Sampler(model, r_sample=100.0)
particles = sampler.sample(100_000, seed=1)
particles.position.shape, particles.velocity.shape, particles.units

```

```
((100000, 3),
 (100000, 3),
 {'position': 'internal', 'velocity': 'internal', 'mass': 'internal'})

```

The same seed gives the same particles. The enclosed mass of the draw follows the profile: for the Hernquist model the mass inside r is proportional to r^2 / (1 + r)^2.

```
r = np.linalg.norm(particles.position, axis=1)
radii = np.array([0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 3.0, 10.0, 30.0])
drawn = np.array([(r < x).mean() for x in radii])
exact = (radii**2 / (1 + radii) ** 2) / (100.0**2 / 101.0**2)
np.column_stack([radii, drawn, exact])

```

```
array([[1.00000000e-01, 8.72000000e-03, 8.43057851e-03],
       [3.00000000e-01, 5.43700000e-02, 5.43248521e-02],
       [1.00000000e+00, 2.57090000e-01, 2.55025000e-01],
       [3.00000000e+00, 5.73190000e-01, 5.73806250e-01],
       [1.00000000e+01, 8.40350000e-01, 8.43057851e-01],
       [3.00000000e+01, 9.53980000e-01, 9.55348595e-01]])

```

The particles are written to a file and read back. The default layout is the package’s own HDF5 file; the layouts of simulation codes are chosen by layout.

```
import tempfile, os

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "hernquist.h5")
particles.write(path)
pp.read(path).identity == particles.identity

```

```
True

```

# Accuracy by release

Every release reruns the same accuracy grid (Accuracy tables) and publishes it as a CSV. The table
counts the grid’s values by tier, its refusals and the cells below the cusp bound, and lists each release’s CSV; a cell that moves beyond its tier between
two releases is a regression by construction.

# Release notes

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/changelog

# Release notes

What each version adds, changes and fixes, newest first. A change that moves a number beyond rounding is named
with the size of the move; the standard and the minimum dependencies are listed with each release.

## Ver. 1.0.0

Draft: this entry is final at the release.

The first stable release: the code of ver. 0.9.9 with the citation entry of Chiang+(2026d) and the DOI of the software
release. Changes to the code since ver. 0.9.9 are listed here at the release.

## Ver. 0.9.9

Draft: this entry is final at the release.

The code of the paper that describes the method, Chiang+(2026d) (MNRAS, submitted), released with its arXiv
submission. Ver. 1.0.0 adds the citation entry.

### Added

A report of the numerical accuracy with every result, on the CPU and on the GPU: the relative error of each
check against the goal of \(10^{-6}\), the ceiling of \(10^{-4}\) and the hard limit of \(10^{-2}\)
(Accuracy); the accuracy grid of the release is on Accuracy tables, and every release’s on
Accuracy by release.

The observables as calls of their own: sigma_r, sigma_t, losvd, aperture_losvd and pdf_v
(the local speed distribution at a 3D radius), beside sigma_los and sigma_los_aperture; every
observable carries its tier.

Ranged draws: a range of radii for Sampler (r_range), a range of speeds at given radii
(Sampler.speeds, v_range), and the projected sampler of \((R, V_{\rm los})\) pairs (ProjectedSampler).

The likelihood of the inference is differentiable in the superposition weights, the unit scales and the
anisotropy parameters \((\beta_{\rm c}, R_{\rm a})\) of the constant, Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt (COM) Type I and Osipkov-Merritt families; and,
through pp.Differentiable, the seven observables as JAX functions of those parameters
(End-to-end differentiability).

The inference fits a superposition to Gauss-Hermite moments (h3, h4), at points or averaged over
apertures, beside the binned data; a free component with moment data is refused, as with binned data.

likelihood, Data, ProjectedSampler and Particles are exported by the package; the gradient
functions (pianistpy.df.gradient) and pianistpy.observables.stages.speed_distribution have entries in
the API reference.

The package includes its type information (py.typed) and its test suite, run on an installation with
pytest --pyargs pianistpy (the test extra installs pytest); the repository has a citation file.

### Changed

The lowered center’s map evaluates its two large, nearly equal terms with expm1 and log1p: the center
now converges in 20 iterations with no floor; no value of the accuracy ledger moves beyond \(1.8 \times 10^{-15}\).

The Gauss-Hermite moments’ edge rule is set by the moment’s own scale (the superposed moments’ edge points move
by at most \(3.7 \times 10^{-10}\)).

Every inner cut of the distribution function’s solve is taken from the inputs (no fixed constant).

The anisotropy factor and its radial derivatives have one form, read by every part of the solve; a Type II
radius at or beyond \(R_{\rm a}\) is refused by name where small clamps stood before, and a Type II truncation whose edge
lies at or beyond \(R_{\rm a}\) is refused after the solve (TYPE II EDGE).

The smallest truncation energy of a Type II distribution function bounded by its domain edge (k_t_min) is
the next float above \(P(R_{\rm a})\), the smallest the strict gate admits.

The slope check of an untruncated Type II distribution function leaves out the first node of its support, where
the function diverges as \((\mathcal{K} - P(R_{\rm a}))^{-1/2}\) and a one-sided difference misreads it by \(2.2 \times 10^{-3}\); the record
states the node left out. Seven models of the accuracy ledger move from warning to goal; no tolerance changes.

The density round trip of a truncated model is read on every row of the edge approach, where a sampling of
radii could miss a peak a few rows wide.

The observables’ worker processes run on the CPU whatever the platform of the calling process.

The minimum versions of the dependencies are found by test, one package at a time and then as one environment,
and listed on Install (NumPy 2.3, SciPy 1.15, h5py 3.11, Astropy 6.1, JAX 0.6, Python 3.11);
Astropy below 7.2 needs NumPy below 2.4. filelock is no longer a dependency.

The examples of the observables’ guide pages use a Hernquist model with a constant anisotropy of 0.25, and
The prepared table states the cost of its example.

The rows of the line-of-sight table are computed in blocks sized to the per-core cache (n_block_elements
25000, was 250000): the rows are the same to the bit, and the table builds in about half the wall time.

The rows of the line-of-sight table take 12 sightline nodes a panel (n_sightline_nodes, was 16): a row
moves by at most \(3.7 \times 10^{-9}\) of its peak (\(4.2 \times 10^{-7}\) at the innermost rows of the
\(\beta_{\rm c} = -0.5\) model of Fig. 15, where 16 and 24 nodes differ by as much), the central and aperture
distributions by at most \(3.7 \times 10^{-10}\), pdf_v and
sigma_los not at all; the anisotropic tables of Fig. 15 build in 14 to 18 percent less wall time.

Python 3.11 is the oldest supported (NumPy 2.3, the oldest NumPy that passes the suite, needs it); JAX is
capped below 0.10.2, on which one test of the suite fails.

One exception class per kind of refusal: AccuracyError carries the refused model (result), as
UnphysicalModelError carries its DF; the sampler’s refusals beyond its limits are AccuracyError (were
ResultError), a model of infinite mass at its sampling UnphysicalModelError, and an existing file at
write InputError for every writer.

A result file is read back after it is written and refused unless it holds what was written, to the bit, as
the particle files are.

A report read from a file is checked against the reports of its kind: a check no such report has is refused
by name, and a check the file lacks (an earlier version made fewer) reads as not judged, so a ver. 0.9.0 file loads
and says what it lacks. An untruncated model’s outer join and eps, which its closed-form profile does not
measure, are not judged (they read 0 before).

Anisotropy stores kind="I" where r_a is infinite, since the type does not enter the model there,
so the same model has one identity.

pianistpy.numerics no longer exports bell_partitions and derivative_from_log, which nothing in the
package used.

The rows of the line-of-sight table end at the first row beyond which less than losvd.outer_mass_share of
the total projected mass lies (the accuracy goal by default; 0 keeps them to the model’s edge), and start at the
profile’s innermost row unless losvd.innermost_read_radius names the smallest projected radius the table will
be read at (The prepared table). Every row kept is the row the full table holds at its radius.

### Fixed

A read of the line-of-sight table beyond its last row or inside its first, at a point, was extrapolated from
the nearest rows; it is refused by name, with the row’s radius and the setting that moves it, as the annulus
read was.

A truncation whose solve reaches its outer radius with no edge is refused by name (NO EDGE, with the radius,
the potential and its slope there); before, it was returned as a truncated model. A component on a parent
profile that is not spatially finite is refused by name.

At an inner slope near 2 with a positive \(\beta_{\rm c}\), the inversion’s table reaches the depth the host’s smallest
radius allows, and these models build where they were refused; the distribution function’s validity is checked
at that depth. A central series that degenerates (\(\gamma = 2\beta_{\rm c}\) at the center) is refused by name
(CENTRAL SERIES).

At an inner slope near 2 the inner extension’s radius no longer underflows to zero; where it lies below the
double’s range the solve is refused by name.

COM Type II models at an inner slope near 2 no longer fail in the inversion with non-finite slopes.

A cusp at the marginal anisotropy \(2\beta_{\rm c} = \gamma\) solves its central deficit: on NFW with \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0.5\) the
density from the distribution function moves from \(7.7 \times 10^{-4}\) to \(3.2 \times 10^{-9}\) of the profile (warning to goal).

The line-of-sight velocity distribution near the center reads the distribution function by the solve’s depth:
one unit in the last place of the potential moved it by \(1.1 \times 10^{-4}\) at \(R_{\rm 2D} = 10^{-9}\), now by \(1.6 \times 10^{-15}\) or less.

The lowest row of the truncated density continues the edge law (it read \(2.5 \times 10^{-4}\) above it).

DistributionFunction.from_function reads the function below the written floor as compute_df does: the
Plummer and Hernquist closed forms are read back with a density round trip of \(2.0 \times 10^{-14}\) and \(4.6 \times 10^{-11}\) (1.0 before).

The particle sampler’s speed table reads its rows at their exact depths and its first slope from the rule below
it; on the speed tables of the Fig. 7 models of Chiang+(2026d) with \(\beta_{\rm c} = 1/2\) the worst row falls from \(4.1 \times 10^{-4}\) to \(1.7 \times 10^{-6}\). Where
the table stops at its row cap above the goal, its log line and the sampler say why.

The pilot grids keep one node at their seam (two nodes \(7 \times 10^{-18}\) apart at \(q = 0.05\) before).

A product of the earlier pipeline whose potential does not strictly decrease is refused when it is loaded, with
the first two rows where it rises and the number of such steps.

The critical band carries the parent’s central deficit to its cubic term, each term from the deficit’s own
integral, and its range reads the deficit’s truncation: where the band meets the rows on the
Fig. 7 children with \(\beta_{\rm c} = 1/2\) the step in \(\log_{10} F\) falls from \(2.5 \times 10^{-6}\) to \(7.9 \times 10^{-9}\) or less; one member of the
accuracy ledger moves (its roundtrip median by 2.3 percent), and no tier changes.

The environment’s switches read one set of words in any case: PIANISTPY_TIMING=false is off (it turned the
timing on), PIANISTPY_VERBOSITY=INFO is info (it raised at import), and an unknown value is refused by
name.

### Known limitations

One component per model at the public calls; several components in one potential are planned
(Upcoming features).

The gradient in the anisotropy parameters refuses COM Type II, whose interior point moves with \(R_{\rm a}\).

The gradient in the anisotropy parameters refuses a Method I truncated model, whose profile moves with them; a
Method II model on a fixed parent takes it (End-to-end differentiability).

On a GPU, the derivative of losvd and aperture_losvd may refuse a row of the line-of-sight table by name
(its transpose holds the row recomputed to the forward’s bit for bit); it never returns a wrong number
(End-to-end differentiability).

Spherical, non-rotating systems with an analytical double-power-law parent profile.

Dependencies: the standard and the minimum lists on Install.

## Ver. 0.9.0

A pre-release with the whole public interface: the distribution functions and their truncation
(compute_df, truncate, solve), the particles, the observables, the superposition and the inference.

Standard dependencies (the versions this release was developed and tested with): Python 3.11.13, NumPy
2.4.3, SciPy 1.17.1, h5py 3.15.1, Astropy 7.2.0, mpmath 1.3.0, SymPy 1.14.0, JAX 0.9.2, Diffrax 0.7.2,
Optimistix 0.1.0, filelock 4.0.12.

Minimum dependencies (the oldest versions that pass the full test suite, measured one package at a time):
Python 3.10; NumPy 2.0.0; SciPy 1.14.0; h5py 3.11.0; Astropy 7.2.0; mpmath 0.17; SymPy 1.2; JAX 0.6.1 with
Diffrax 0.7.0 and Optimistix 0.0.11 (these three are bound together); filelock. On Python 3.10 the newest JAX
is 0.6.2 (JAX 0.7 and later need Python 3.11). GPU: jax[cuda12] from 0.4.38 passes the suite on a GPU node;
the declared bound is the joint one above. Python 3.12 and 3.13 pass.

     On this page

# How to cite

citation entry, the arXiv link and the DOI of the software release are added with ver. 1.0.0.

# Contributing

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/project/contributing

# Contributing

Bug reports, questions and proposed changes are welcome on the
issue tracker.

## Reporting a problem

Please include the version (pianistpy.__version__), the inputs that reproduce the problem (the profile, the
anisotropy, the truncation and the settings) and the full error message. An error raised by the package ends with
its most recent log messages; please keep them in the report. For a result that came with an accuracy warning,
please include its validation report.

## Setting up

```
git clone https://github.com/barrytchiang/PIANISTpy.git
cd PIANISTpy
python -m pip install -e .
python -m pip install pytest ruff mypy

```

## Before proposing a change

Read STYLE_GUIDE.md in the repository. It covers the names, the docstrings, the units, the numerical rules
and the checklist that every change is held to.

Run the formatter and the linter (ruff format, ruff check, mypy).

Run the tests, which include the examples in the docstrings (python -m pytest).

Add a test for the change: a new function comes with a test of its result against an independent
reference, a closed form, a limit, or an identity that the result must satisfy.

## Rules for pull requests

One quantity, one function. Each quantity is computed by exactly one function; a second route to the same
number replaces the first rather than sitting beside it.

No silent changes to results. A change that moves a result beyond rounding states the size of the move and
its reason.

Runtime options leave results unchanged. Verbosity, timing and the number of workers never alter what is
computed.

Accuracy is verified, not assumed. A numerical setting joins a tested tier only after passing that tier’s
checks.

LLM-assisted development. Code written with the help of large language models is permitted and
encouraged. The contributor must review every change, and the pull request description itself, thoroughly
before submitting; a pull request that shows it was not reviewed this way is rejected outright.

     On this page
