# T:2 The distribution function

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/df

# T:2 The distribution function

## T:2.1 The inversion

Chiang+(2026d) gives the inversion in two forms: with the derivative outside the integral, Eq. (B22), and with the derivative inside the integral together with a surface term at \(P = 0\), Eq. (B9). The second form follows from the first by one integration by parts and is simpler to evaluate. The integration by parts requires that

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}^m\varrho_\mathrm{aux}}{\mathrm{d} P^m}\ \text{continuous on}\ [0, \mathcal{K}] \qquad\text{and}\qquad \int_0^{\mathcal{K}}\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}^{m+1}\varrho_\mathrm{aux}}{\mathrm{d} P^{m+1}}\right|(\mathcal{K}-P)^{-n}\,\mathrm{d} P < \infty .
  \tag{T:2.1}
\end{equation}
Neither condition is guaranteed. The first can fail at the outer end, \(P = 0\) (Section T:2.2.6), and at the anisotropy radius of a Type II model (Section T:2.2.8).

For half-integer \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) we have \(n = 0\), and the general form reduces to a derivative with no integral,

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{K}) = \frac{2^{\beta_\mathrm{c}}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}^m\varrho_\mathrm{aux}}{\mathrm{d} P^m}\right|_{P=\mathcal{K}} .
  \tag{T:2.2}
\end{equation}
The forward relation is a Volterra equation whose lower limit lies at \(P = 0\), that is, at \(R = \infty\):

\begin{equation}
  \varrho_\mathrm{aux}(P) = \frac{2\pi^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}{\Gamma(3/2-\beta_\mathrm{c})} \int_0^{P} F_\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{K})\,\left[2(P - \mathcal{K})\right]^{1/2-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K} .
  \tag{T:2.3}
\end{equation}

## T:2.2 Asymptotic behavior of the DF

### T:2.2.1 The center: the singular part of one power-law term

Consider a single term \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \supset A_s\,(P_0 - P)^{s}\) of the expansion of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) about the center. Its \((m+1)\)-th derivative is \((-1)^{m+1} A_s\,[\Gamma(s+1)/\Gamma(s-m)]\,(P_0-P)^{s-m-1}\). With \(t = \mathcal{K} - P\), the integral of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B9) becomes \(\int_0^{\mathcal{K}} t^{-n} (u+t)^{s-m-1}\,\mathrm{d} t\), whose behavior as \(u \to 0\) follows from the Mellin-type integral

\begin{equation}
  \int_0^{\infty} t^{a-1}(u+t)^{-b}\,\mathrm{d} t = u^{a-b}\,\frac{\Gamma(a)\,\Gamma(b-a)}{\Gamma(b)},
  \tag{T:2.4}
\end{equation}
with \(a = 1-n\) and \(b = m+1-s\). The finite upper limit adds only a part that is analytic at \(u = 0\). Using \(\Gamma(s-m)\,\Gamma(m+1-s) = \pi/\sin[\pi(s-m)]\) and \(\Gamma(-s)\,\Gamma(1+s) = -\pi/\sin(\pi s)\), the term contributes

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K}^{\rm sing}(\mathcal{K}) = \frac{2^{\beta_\mathrm{c}}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\; A_s\,\frac{\Gamma(\nu - s)}{\Gamma(-s)}\; u^{\,s-\nu},
  \tag{T:2.5}
\end{equation}
plus a part that is analytic in \(u\). Three properties of Eq. (T:2.5) decide what follows.

For \(s\) a non-negative integer, \(1/\Gamma(-s) = 0\), and the term has no singular part.

For \(s = \nu + k\) with \(k\) a non-negative integer and \(\nu\) not an integer, \(\Gamma(\nu - s)\) has a pole, and the power is replaced by a logarithm,

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K}^{\rm sing}(\mathcal{K}) = \frac{2^{\beta_\mathrm{c}}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\,\frac{(-1)^{k}\,A_s}{k!\;\Gamma(-s)}\;u^{k}\,(-\ln u) ,
  \tag{T:2.6}
\end{equation}
which for \(k = 0\) reduces to \(-\,2^{\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,A_\nu\,\ln u\,/\,[(2\pi)^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})\,\Gamma(-\nu)]\).

Otherwise the term is a power law \(u^{\,s-\nu}\), whose sign is that of \(A_s\,\Gamma(\nu-s)/\Gamma(-s)\).

Since the inversion is linear, every power in the expansion of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) contributes its own term of the form Eq. (T:2.5) or Eq. (T:2.6), and the singular part of \(F_\mathcal{K}\) at the center is the sum of these terms in order of increasing \(s\). Only the non-negative integer powers drop out; a negative integer \(s\) is singular like any other. The coefficients \(A_s\) follow from the expansion of Section T:1.1. A ratio of two Gamma functions is formed as the exponential of a difference of log-Gamma values together with its sign, never as a direct quotient, so that a steep center whose Gamma values overflow still has a finite amplitude.

### T:2.2.2 The regular branch, \(\gamma > 2\beta_\mathrm{c}\)

The leading term of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) is \(A\,(P_0-P)^{s_0}\) with \(s_0 = (2\beta_\mathrm{c} - \gamma)/(2-\gamma) < 0\). Eq. (T:2.5) reproduces the exponent \(\kappa\) of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B36) and supplies its amplitude,

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K} \simeq \frac{2^{\beta_\mathrm{c}}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\,A\,\frac{\Gamma(\nu - s_0)}{\Gamma(-s_0)}\,u^{\kappa},
  \tag{T:2.7}
\end{equation}
which is positive. For the isotropic Hernquist profile in units \(G = M = a = 1\), \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \simeq (2\pi u)^{-1}\) and \(F \simeq 3\,u^{-5/2}/(16\sqrt{2}\,\pi^2)\), which is the leading term of its known closed form.

As \(\gamma \to 2\beta_\mathrm{c}\), the amplitude vanishes linearly, \(\Gamma(\nu - s_0)/\Gamma(-s_0) = -s_0\,\Gamma(\nu) + \mathcal{O}(s_0^2)\), while the exponent tends to \(-\nu\). The regular and the critical branch therefore join in amplitude but not in exponent.

### T:2.2.3 The critical branch, \(\gamma = 2\beta_\mathrm{c}\)

By Eq. (T:1.1), \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} = C_1 + C_2\,(P_0-P)^{\delta} + \dots\) is a series in \((P_0-P)^{\delta}\). The constant term has \(s = 0\) and no singular part. The next term has \(s = \delta\) and the exponent \(\kappa' = \delta - \nu\) of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B37). Table T:2.1 lists the cases; its last four rows assume that \(\delta\) is not an integer.

Table T:2.1. The central DF in the critical case \(\gamma = 2\beta_\mathrm{c}\), for constant anisotropy and OM models.

Condition

Central behavior

Leading form

\(\delta\) a positive integer

finite

analytic in \(u\)

\(\kappa' < 0\)

power-law divergence

Eq. (T:2.5) with \(s = \delta\), \(A_s = C_2\)

\(\kappa' = 0\)

logarithmic divergence

Eq. (T:2.6) with \(A_\nu = C_2\)

\(\kappa' > 0\), \(n \neq 0\)

finite, non-zero

\(F_\mathcal{K}(P_0) + \mathcal{O}(u^{\kappa'})\)

\(\kappa' > 0\), \(n = 0\)

vanishing

\(\propto u^{\kappa'}\)

Sign. With \(C_2 < 0\), the divergence is toward negative values for \(1 < \delta < \nu\), and also for \(\kappa' = 0\) with \(\beta_\mathrm{c} < 1/2\). Such models are unphysical even though they satisfy Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (12).

The finite case at \(\kappa' = 0\). This case requires \(\delta = \nu\) to be an integer. Within \(0 \leq \gamma < 2\) it occurs only for \(\alpha = 1\), \(\gamma = 1\), \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 1/2\), which includes the NFW and Hernquist profiles.

The local case. For \(n = 0\) the inversion is the derivative of Eq. (T:2.2), and the non-local constant \(F_\mathcal{K}(P_0)\) is absent.

### T:2.2.4 COM models

For COM models, the factor \((1 \pm R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2)^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) contributes a series in \(R^2 \propto (P_0-P)^{2/(2-\gamma)}\). The expansion of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) then contains the powers

\begin{equation}
  s_{kj} = k\,\delta + \frac{2j}{2-\gamma}, \qquad k, j \geq 0,
  \tag{T:2.8}
\end{equation}
and the leading singular term is the smallest \(s_{kj}\) that is not an integer. The result of Section T:2.2.3 is modified when \(2/(2-\gamma)\) is not an integer and, in addition, either \(2/(2-\gamma) < \delta\) or \(\delta\) is an integer. Since \(2/(2-\gamma)\) is an integer at \(\gamma = 0\) and at \(\gamma = 1\), OM models (which are critical only at \(\gamma = 0\)) and all \(\gamma = 1\) profiles are unaffected.

Where the modification applies, the exponent is \(2/(2-\gamma) - \nu\), which is negative for \(0 < \gamma < (5-\sqrt{17})/2 \simeq 0.438\). A center that is finite under constant anisotropy is then divergent under COM Type I. For example, \((\alpha, \gamma, \beta_\mathrm{c}) = (1.8, 0.2, 0.1)\) has \(\delta = 1\) and a finite center under constant anisotropy, but \(F_\mathcal{K} \propto u^{-13/45}\) under COM Type I.

### T:2.2.5 The NFW profile at \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 1/2\)

With \(\varrho = 1/[R(1+R)^2]\) and \(P = \ln(1+R)/R\), Eq. (T:2.2) gives

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K} = \frac{1}{2\pi^2}\frac{\mathrm{d}(R\varrho)}{\mathrm{d} P} = \frac{1}{\pi^2}\,\frac{R^2}{(1+R)^3\left[\ln(1+R) - R/(1+R)\right]},
  \tag{T:2.9}
\end{equation}
evaluated at \(R(\mathcal{K})\). Its expansion about the center contains integer powers only,

\begin{equation}
  \pi^2 F_\mathcal{K} = 2 - \frac{20}{3}u + \frac{28}{3}u^2 - \frac{1024}{135}u^3 + \mathcal{O}(u^4),
  \tag{T:2.10}
\end{equation}
so the central DF is finite, \(F_\mathcal{K}(P_0) = 2/\pi^2\).

### T:2.2.6 The outer end, \(P = 0\)

Let \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \propto P^{\,y}\) as \(P \to 0\). Then \(\mathrm{d}^m\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d} P^m \propto P^{\,y-m}\), and the surface term of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B9)

\begin{equation}
  \text{vanishes for}\ y > m, \qquad \text{is finite for}\ y = m, \qquad \text{diverges for}\ y < m .
  \tag{T:2.11}
\end{equation}
For an untruncated profile with \(\beta > 3\), Eq. (T:1.2) gives

\begin{equation}
  y = \beta - 2\beta_\mathrm{c} \ \ \text{(constant anisotropy)}, \qquad y = \beta - 2 \ \ \text{[(C)OM Type~I]}.
  \tag{T:2.12}
\end{equation}
Table T:2.2 lists the consequences. The bound \(\beta > m+2\) is sharp.

Table T:2.2. The surface term at \(P = 0\) for untruncated profiles with \(\beta > 3\).

Model

\(m\)

Surface term vanishes

constant anisotropy

\(\lfloor 3/2 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\rfloor\)

always

(C)OM Type I, \(\beta_\mathrm{c} > 1/2\)

0

always

(C)OM Type I, \(-1/2 < \beta_\mathrm{c} \leq 1/2\)

1

always

(C)OM Type I, \(\beta_\mathrm{c} \leq -1/2\)

\(\geq 2\)

for \(\beta > m + 2\)

At \(\beta = 3\) the constant-anisotropy surface term still vanishes. For (C)OM Type I, \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \propto P/\ln(1/P)\), so the term vanishes only as \(1/\ln(1/P)\) for \(m = 1\) and diverges for \(m \geq 2\). For \(2 < \beta < 3\) and \(m = 1\) the term is finite and non-zero.

### T:2.2.7 The tail of the DF and its density

For an untruncated (C)OM Type I model with \(\beta > 3\), Eq. (T:2.12) and Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B25) give a power-law tail,

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{K}) \simeq A\,\mathcal{K}^{-a} \quad (\mathcal{K} \to 0), \qquad a = \nu - (\beta - 2) = \tfrac{7}{2} - \beta_\mathrm{c} - \beta ,
  \tag{T:2.13}
\end{equation}
which diverges for \(a > 0\); a profile with an outer slope of exactly 3 carries a logarithmic factor beside the power. By Eq. (T:2.3), the part of the tail below an energy \(q\) contributes to the auxiliary density at \(P > q\) the amount

\begin{equation}
  \varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{\rm tail}(P) = \frac{2\pi^{3/2}\,\Gamma(1-\beta_\mathrm{c})}{\Gamma(3/2-\beta_\mathrm{c})}\; 2^{\,\nu-1} A\, P^{\,\nu-a}\; B\!\left(\frac{q}{P};\, 1-a,\, \nu\right),
  \tag{T:2.14}
\end{equation}
where \(B(x; p, r) = \int_0^x t^{p-1}(1-t)^{r-1}\,\mathrm{d} t\) is the incomplete Beta function. The integral converges for \(a < 1\). For \(a \geq 1\) the density integral diverges at \(\mathcal{K} = 0\), and the untruncated model does not exist; a truncated model does exist, since the truncated DF of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B27) vanishes at its lower end.

### T:2.2.8 The anisotropy radius of a Type II model

For Type II models, \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} \propto w^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) as \(w \equiv 1 - R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2 \to 0\), and \(w\) is linear in \(P - P(R_\mathrm{a})\) there. Hence

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}^m\varrho_\mathrm{aux}}{\mathrm{d} P^m} \propto |P - P(R_\mathrm{a})|^{\,1-\beta_\mathrm{c}-m} = |P - P(R_\mathrm{a})|^{\,n - 1/2},
  \tag{T:2.15}
\end{equation}
which diverges at \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) for \(n < 1/2\). The divergence is approached from inside \(R_\mathrm{a}\) and does not depend on how \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) is continued beyond it (Section T:3.1). For OM Type II, \(n = 1/2\) and the factor is a polynomial, so the conditions of Eq. (T:2.1) hold. A truncated model with \(R_\mathrm{t} \leq {R_\mathrm{a}}\) does not contain the point at all.

## T:2.3 The form of every row

### T:2.3.1 The order pair and the choice of form

The form of the inversion is fixed from the model parameters alone, before any integral is evaluated.

Order pair. From \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) the code forms the pair \((m, n)\) of Eq. (T:0.1). For \(n > 1/2\) it replaces the pair by

\begin{equation}
  (j, n') = (m+1,\; n-1),
  \tag{T:2.16}
\end{equation}
so that the kernel exponent always satisfies \(|n'| \leq 1/2\); otherwise \((j, n') = (m, n)\). With the higher order, the surface term can diverge as \(P \to 0\) (Section T:2.2.6) and cancel against the integral, so a replaced pair is evaluated in the general form, Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B22), on every row.

Half-integer \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\). For \(n = 0\) the closed form of Eq. (T:2.2) is used, and no quadrature is performed.

Interior point. For an untruncated COM Type II model, the point \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) and the exponent of Eq. (T:2.15) are known in closed form. Rows with \(\mathcal{K} < P(R_\mathrm{a})\) use the form with the surface term, Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B9); rows above it use the general form, with the integral split at \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) and a Gauss-Jacobi rule on either side that carries the exponent as its weight. For odd integer \(1-\beta_\mathrm{c}\) the factor is a polynomial, and there is no such point.

An unbounded outer end. Where \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}\) is unbounded at \(P = 0\), the rows above a stated energy use the general form.

All other rows use the form with the surface term.

Applying the same operator one derivative higher gives \(\mathrm{d} F_\mathcal{K}/\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K}\) on the same rows, so the table carries an exact slope column.

### T:2.3.2 The floor of the table

The table of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) and its derivatives starts at a floor \(q_0 > 0\), not at \(P = 0\). Splitting the integral of the general form at \(q_0\) and integrating its upper part by parts gives, with no assumption about the behavior at \(P = 0\),

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K}}\int_0^{\mathcal{K}}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n}}\,\mathrm{d} P = \int_{q_0}^{\mathcal{K}}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j+1)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n}}\,\mathrm{d} P + \frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(q_0)}{(\mathcal{K}-q_0)^{n}} - n\int_0^{q_0}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n+1}}\,\mathrm{d} P ,
  \tag{T:2.17}
\end{equation}
where \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)} \equiv {\mathrm{d}}^j\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d} P^j\). The first two terms need only the table. The third term is the contribution of the stretch below the floor. In Method I it is evaluated from the exact derivatives of Section T:1.2.1 on Gauss-Legendre nodes in \(\ln P\), down to a lower limit far below \(q_0\), so that the floor of the table is not the floor of the model; in Method II it is the closed form of Section T:2.6. The default floor is \(q_0 = 10^{-10}\) in units of the central potential, and untruncated DF tables are written from \(2\,q_0\) upward.

### T:2.3.3 The general form on a split

Rows that use the general form (Section T:2.3.1) split the integral at an interior point \(c < \mathcal{K}\). Below \(c\) the derivative is taken under the integral sign; above \(c\) the integral is integrated by parts:

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K}}\int_{q_0}^{\mathcal{K}}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n}}\,\mathrm{d} P = -n\int_{q_0}^{c}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n+1}}\,\mathrm{d} P + \frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}(c)}{(\mathcal{K}-c)^{n}} + \int_{c}^{\mathcal{K}}\frac{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j+1)}(P)}{(\mathcal{K}-P)^{n}}\,\mathrm{d} P .
  \tag{T:2.18}
\end{equation}
The right-hand side requires \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j)}\) only where it is bounded, and \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(j+1)}\) only above \(c\). For a replaced pair, Eq. (T:2.16), this avoids \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(m+1)}\) at the floor, which the form with the surface term would require and which can diverge as \(P \to 0\). For rows above the interior point of a COM Type II model, \(c\) lies above \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\), and the lower integral is evaluated on the two sides of that point with a rule that carries the exponent of Eq. (T:2.15) as its weight.

### T:2.3.4 Quadrature

Each row is integrated on three sub-intervals: from the floor to one tenth of the split point, on nodes uniform in \(\ln P\); from there to the split point \(c = 0.9\,\mathcal{K}\), on Gauss-Legendre nodes; and from the split point to \(\mathcal{K}\), where the kernel is singular. On the last sub-interval the integration variable is \(v\), with

\begin{equation}
  P = P_0 - (P_0 - \mathcal{K})\,e^{y}, \qquad y = v^{k}, \qquad k = \frac{1}{1-n} .
  \tag{T:2.19}
\end{equation}
Near the upper limit, \(\mathcal{K} - P \simeq (P_0 - \mathcal{K})\,y\), so that

\begin{equation}
  (\mathcal{K} - P)^{-n}\,\mathrm{d} P \;\propto\; y^{-n}\,\mathrm{d} y = k\,v^{\,k(1-n)-1}\,\mathrm{d} v = k\,\mathrm{d} v ,
  \tag{T:2.20}
\end{equation}
and the kernel singularity is removed for every exponent that the order pair allows. Away from the upper limit, the nodes are uniform in \(\ln(P_0 - P)\), which resolves an integrand that steepens as a power of \(P_0 - P\) toward the center.

## T:2.4 The energy grid

The DF is tabulated on a grid of energies in five zones, from the floor to the gap below the central potential: zone A, logarithmic in \(\mathcal{K}\) from the floor; zone AB, a buffer; zone B, linear; zone BC, a buffer; and zone C, logarithmic in \(P_0 - \mathcal{K}\) up to the gap. A buffer carries the step geometrically from the spacing on one side to the spacing on the other. Its number of steps is the one whose total comes closest to the width of the buffer, and the steps are rescaled to sum to that width exactly, so that no jump in spacing enters the rows. The linear zone and the two logarithmic zones take their row counts from the settings, and the logarithmic zones extend over a stated fraction of the central potential. An OM Type I model places zones A and AB around the potential of its anisotropy radius; an OM Type II or COM model places them around the feature that a pilot inversion on a coarse grid finds (the minimum or the zero crossing of its DF), refined by a parabola through the neighboring nodes. The upper end is never moved. Below the floor, the grid is extended at a stated number of nodes per decade down to the table’s own floor, where the rule below the table takes over (Section T:2.5.4). A grid whose energies are not strictly increasing in double precision is refused.

## T:2.5 Beyond the table

### T:2.5.1 Where the rows end

The rows end at the last energy of the grid, a gap of \(10^{-9}\) below \(P_0\), unless the exact derivatives required by the inversion cannot be formed that deep. Each term \(C_s u^{s}\) of the central series of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) gives \(\mathrm{d}^N\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d} P^N = (-1)^N C_s\, s(s-1)\cdots(s-N+1)\,u^{s-N}\), which exceeds the largest double below \(u = (|C_s\,s\cdots(s-N+1)|/\mathrm{DBL\_MAX})^{1/(N-s)}\) for \(s < N\). The largest such depth over the terms and over the orders that the form needs is the top limit of the table, and it is zero where no term grows. The rows end at the shallower of that depth and the depth at the smallest radius whose square the host represents (Section T:0.4); the closed form of the center owns the energies above. Where the leading exponent of the series vanishes (\(\gamma = 2\beta_\mathrm{c}\) at the center), there is no closed form to join to, and a model whose host floor alone would cut its table is refused with a named reason.

### T:2.5.2 Above the top of the table

The table of \(F_\mathcal{K}\) ends at a top node, a small depth \(u_{\rm top}\) below the center. Between that node and the center, the DF is continued by its central form, Section T:2.2.1 to Section T:2.2.4, which is computed from the model alone and stored with the table. The stored form consists of the leading singular term \(S_1(u)\) and the next one, \(S_2(u)\), each a power or a logarithm with the coefficient of Eq. (T:2.5) or Eq. (T:2.6). The coefficients of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) that they need come from the exact expansion of Section T:1.1, carried to the second power that is not a non-negative integer. No exponent is fitted to the table, and the amplitude is the closed form wherever the center states one.

What remains of \(F_\mathcal{K}\) once the two singular terms are removed is analytic in \(u\), and it changes across the gap by a relative amount of order \(u_{\rm top}\). It is therefore held at its value at the top node,

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K}(u) = S_1(u) + S_2(u) + \left[F_\mathcal{K}(u_{\rm top}) - S_1(u_{\rm top}) - S_2(u_{\rm top})\right], \qquad u < u_{\rm top} .
  \tag{T:2.21}
\end{equation}
Two cases depart from Eq. (T:2.21). Where the leading power is positive and the inversion is local (the last row of Table T:2.1), \(F_\mathcal{K}\) vanishes at the center, and the bracket is multiplied by \(u/u_{\rm top}\) so that the continuation vanishes with it. Where the center is analytic, there is no singular term, and \(F_\mathcal{K}\) is held at its top value. For a divergent power, the expression is evaluated in logarithms relative to \(S_1\), so that a DF whose central values exceed the range of double precision is continued without overflow.

Where the rows end below the gap (Section T:2.5.1), the node at which the form takes over is called the anchor. The regular part is then a fit \(B + D u\) to the rows below the anchor, over a window that widens until the three-term and the four-term fits agree in amplitude to one tenth of the goal; the singular exponent is never fitted. A band of rows at the top that is not positive is excluded only where the form holds there, as judged by the local slope \(\mathrm{d}\ln F/\mathrm{d}\ln u\) against \(\kappa\).

A truncated Method I model has \(\hat{F}_\mathcal{K}(\hat{\mathcal{K}}) = F_\mathcal{K}(\hat{\mathcal{K}} + \mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}) - F_\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t})\), which differs from the untruncated DF by a constant. Its singular terms and their coefficients are those of the untruncated model, with \(u\) measured from the truncated central potential.

The stored form is tested against the table that it continues. Across the top decade of the table, \(u_{\rm top} \leq u \leq 10\,u_{\rm top}\), the table less its singular terms may change only by the variation of the analytic part. A change above the accuracy goal is reported with the product; a change above the hard limit means that the stored form belongs to a different model, and the product is refused.

### T:2.5.3 Below the floor

Below its first energy, the DF follows a stated rule that is recorded with the table: the tail \(A\,\mathcal{K}^{-a}[\ln(E_0/\mathcal{K})]^{-b}\) of Eq. (T:2.13) for an untruncated model, with its amplitude taken from the boundary term of Eq. (T:2.17) at the floor; the Taylor form \(F_1\mathcal{K} + F_2\mathcal{K}^2/2\) of a truncated Method I model at its edge, together with the energy up to which it holds; the edge law \(\mathcal{K}^{p}(C_0 + C_1\mathcal{K})\) of a Method II child (Section T:2.6.1); or zero. The integral of the rule from zero up to an energy below the table is the same set of numbers in closed form, so a density integral never truncates the DF at its table.

### T:2.5.4 The lookup

Inside the table, the base-10 logarithm of the DF is the cubic Hermite interpolant in \(\ln{\mathcal{K}}\) through the nodes with the exact slope column. Where a table carries no exact slopes (a DF from a function, Section T:2.7), the slopes are those of the not-a-knot spline through the nodes. The lookup has two entry points, by the energy and by the depth \(u = P_0 - \mathcal{K}\), and a caller asks by whichever argument it holds exactly. For example, a speed draw near the top holds the depth \(u = (P_0 - \Psi) + \Psi x^2\) exactly, whereas the energy \(\Psi(1 - x^2)\) formed in doubles loses it. In the entry by \(u\), the cell position is formed from \(u_i - u\) with \(u_i = P_0 - \mathcal{K}_i\), which is exact for \(\mathcal{K}_i \geq P_0/2\), and the form above the table is read at \(u\) itself. The nodes and every number of the forms are arrays, so that under JAX the table is a traced argument, and two tables with the same node bucket and the same kinds of forms share one compiled function.

### T:2.5.5 What a table states about itself

A table is written together with its checks: the stated slope column against the table’s own \(F\), the stated center against the top decade of the table, and the joins of the forms below the floor with the bottom row. A reader refuses a table that fails any of these beyond the hard limit. The sign report states where the DF is negative and the smallest truncation above which it is not (Section T:3.5). The validity certificate is a closed form: from the model and the central exponent, it states whether the columns of the table are representable in double precision over the energies that it would need, judged at the deepest of the gap, the top limit, and the host floor.

## T:2.6 A component on a tabulated pair (Method II)

Method II is not a second pipeline. A component whose profile is the truncated profile of another model runs through the same stages, and only the source of the derivatives differs. The density of the parent is the integral of its DF,

\begin{equation}
  \hat\varrho(P) = 4\pi\sqrt{2}\int_0^{P} F(\mathcal{K})\,(P - \mathcal{K})^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K} ,
  \tag{T:2.22}
\end{equation}
so its derivatives with respect to \(P\) are integrals of the DF and of its derivatives against \((P - \mathcal{K})^{-1/2}\), evaluated from the parent’s table, its exact slope column, and its Taylor edge; no spline of the rows is ever differentiated. The auxiliary density of the child is \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux} = h(R)\,\hat\varrho\) with the child’s own factor, and its derivatives follow by the Leibniz rule with \(\mathrm{d} R/\mathrm{d} P\) taken from the rows. Orders up to three are served, the third only where the parent states its Taylor edge. An isotropic or OM Type I parent is served, and a Type II child must have its \(R_\mathrm{a}\) beyond the parent’s edge.

The grid is the five-zone grid of Section T:2.4 on the first potential of the parent, compact, with no extension below the floor, since the support of the child ends at the parent’s edge. The stretch below the floor has a closed form. For each power \(P^{q}\) of the two-term edge expansion of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) (Section T:2.6.1), with \(a = q - m_f\), \(b = 1 - n_f\), and \(x = q_0/\mathcal{K}\),

\begin{equation}
  C(n_f)\,a_q\,\frac{\Gamma(q+1)}{\Gamma(a+1)}\;\mathcal{K}^{\,a-n_f}\,x^{a}\left[{}_2F_1(a, n_f;\, a+1;\, x) - 1\right]
  \tag{T:2.23}
\end{equation}
is the exact contribution of \([0, q_0]\) to the row at \(\mathcal{K}\), relative to the boundary form that the kernel carries, and the exact value of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}^{(m_f)}\) at the floor is the boundary term.

At \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 1/2\) on a parent with \(\gamma = \alpha = 1\), the inversion is a derivative whose two terms are both of order \(1/u\) toward the center, so the rows there carry the parent’s accuracy multiplied by \(1/(4u)\). Above an anchor, the rows are the closed form \(F = A\sum_{k \leq 4} a_k u^{k}\) with \(A = 1/(2\pi^2)\) (Section T:2.2.5), which is exact in the truncation through the parent’s central deficit. The anchor is the smaller of the series’ own range at the goal and the top zone of the grid, and the computed rows over the outermost decade inside it must agree with the form to within the goal; otherwise the anchor steps inward one decade at a time until they do.

### T:2.6.1 The edge of a Method II child

A density that ends as \(P^{q}\) at its edge has a DF of central anisotropy \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) if and only if \(\beta_\mathrm{c} > 1/2 - q\), and the DF then behaves as \(\mathcal{K}^{\,q - 3/2 + \beta_\mathrm{c}}\) there. This statement holds for every profile and every anisotropy model of the package, and a child that violates it is refused before any stage runs, with the admissible range stated. Below the parent’s switch energy, the parent’s DF is its Taylor form \(F_1\mathcal{K} + F_2\mathcal{K}^2/2\), so the parent’s density near the edge is \(4\pi\sqrt{2}\,[\tfrac{4}{15}F_1 P^{5/2} + \tfrac{8}{105}F_2 P^{7/2}]\) to the order kept. The child’s augmented density, with \(h = h_\mathrm{t} + H_1 P\), \(H_1 = h'(R_\mathrm{t})\,R'(P)\), and \(R' = -R_\mathrm{t}^2/M_\mathrm{t}\), is then

\begin{equation}
  \varrho_{\rm aug}(P) = a_{5/2}\,P^{5/2} + a_{7/2}\,P^{7/2} + \mathcal{O}(P^{9/2}) .
  \tag{T:2.24}
\end{equation}
Each power inverts to a power, so the child’s DF below its switch is the edge law \(\mathcal{K}^{p}(C_0 + C_1\mathcal{K})\) with \(p = 1 + \beta_\mathrm{c}\), and the same coefficients give the floor terms of Eq. (T:2.23).

## T:2.7 A distribution function from a function

A DF obtained elsewhere, from a fitting function or from the output of another code, is certified in the same way. Its values on the energy grid that the inversion would place for the component enter at the point where the rows of the inversion would enter, and everything downstream is unchanged: the forms beyond the table, the sign report, the checks, and the record. Such a table has no exact slope column, which its report states, and a value that is not finite is refused, with the first such energy named. Truncation needs the rows of the inversion, which such a table does not carry, and it is refused with a named reason.

     On this page


---

# T:7 Gradients

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/gradients

# T:7 Gradients

## T:7.1 The inversion’s rule

The rows of the inversion are \(F = T_b[g](q)\) on a fixed grid \(q\), where \(T_b\) is the operator of Section T:2.3 with its completion below the floor, applied to the source \(g\), namely the rows of \(\mathrm{d}^N\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d} P^N\). At a fixed central anisotropy \(b = \beta_\mathrm{c}\), the operator is linear in its source, so that

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial F}{\partial {R_\mathrm{a}}} = T_b\!\left[\partial_{R_\mathrm{a}} g\right], \qquad \frac{\partial F}{\partial {\beta_\mathrm{c}}} = T_b\!\left[\partial_{b}\, g\right] + E_b[g] ,
  \tag{T:7.1}
\end{equation}
where \(\partial_\theta g\) denotes the mixed derivatives at fixed \(P\), formed symbolically in the same way as the derivatives of Section T:1.2.1, and \(E_b\) is the derivative of the operator itself with respect to \(b\) at fixed \(g\), through its prefactor and the exponent of its kernel. \(E_b\) has no closed form and is taken from the values of the operator at nearby \(b\): a central Richardson quotient over a step and its half inside the region of one form, or the one-sided third-order combinations of both sides and their mean at a corner where the form changes on one side (half-integer \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\), or the switch of the pair). The step balances the measured accuracy of the kernel against the truncation term of the quotient. The record states the Richardson residual of the quotient and, at a corner, the spread between its two sides, both relative to the scale of the column, and the residual is read in the tiers of Section T:0.5.

The table that the lookup reads is a function of the rows and of closed forms in \(\theta\), so its derivative is the chain rule through each piece, with every discrete choice of the forward pass held fixed: the grid, the anchor, the window of the fit, and the nodes below the written floor. The contribution of the rows is Eq. (T:7.1) along the rows. The form above the anchor is its least-squares fit linearized in the rows, with the exponent \(\kappa(b)\) and the amplitude \(A(b)\) of the center in closed form on the regular branch. The nodes below the floor are the integral, which is linear in its source, with the source’s cubic in \((\ln P, \ln|g|)\) linearized; in \(b\), the exponent and the prefactor of the floor pair are differenced in the same way as \(E_b\). The tail contributes through its amplitude, exponent, and scale from the first node below the floor. On a Method II child the parent is held fixed, and the sources of the child are the Leibniz sum of Section T:2.6, whose derivative is the same sum with \(\partial h/\partial\theta\) in closed form; the leaves are the rows, the edge law, and the stated form of the center, each with its derivative written out. The derivative is that of the solve with its choices fixed; between two parameters at which a choice changes, the solve at the second differs from the held one by its own tolerance.

## T:7.2 What is served

Gradients are served for constant anisotropy (\(\beta_\mathrm{c}\)), Cuddeford Type I (\(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) and \(R_\mathrm{a}\)), and Osipkov-Merritt Type I and II (\(R_\mathrm{a}\)). Three cases are refused, each with a named reason. The first is Cuddeford Type II, whose kernel carries the factor \((P - P(R_\mathrm{a}))^{s}\) with \(s = 1 - \beta_\mathrm{c} - j\), an interior point that moves with \(R_\mathrm{a}\) and an exponent that moves with \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\), so that the derivative of the factor with respect to \(R_\mathrm{a}\) is not integrable at the interior point for \(s \leq 0\), and the mixed rows do not carry the derivative there. The second is a center on its critical branch, where the branch itself changes with \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\). The third is a component on a profile that carries no DF of its own model. The derivative of the observables of a model with respect to \((\beta_\mathrm{c}, R_\mathrm{a})\) is the full derivative for a Method II model, whose profile is held fixed. A truncated Method I model is refused by name, since its profile is that of its own DF and moves with the anisotropy, so that neither the Jeans path at a fixed profile nor the DF’s path at a fixed potential carries the full derivative; an untruncated model is refused on both paths, since its edge terms read its DF.

## T:7.3 The observables’ tangent rows

Each observable is served as a JAX function of \(\theta = (\beta_\mathrm{c}, R_\mathrm{a})\) with a custom derivative. Its value is the public call on the model rebuilt at \(\theta\) on the host, and its derivative is given by the tangent rows of the observable in \(\theta\) on the tables’ own rows, with their placement frozen. The tangent rows of the radial dispersion are the derivative of the Jeans rule Eq. (T:6.1) on the same rows and nodes on the fixed profile, with the limit of the edge reading unmoved. The tangent rows of the projection are the derivative of the line-of-sight rule on the same nodes, through the derivative of the profile’s reading, and zero where the squared dispersion is clipped. The derivative of an aperture is the aperture’s integral of the tangent rows of the squared dispersion on the nodes of the plain call. The velocity distributions take their derivatives through the derivative of the DF itself: the lookup is differentiated by JAX on its own expressions, and the transpose carries a cotangent on \(F\) at the energies back to the numbers of the table through the three maps between them (the padded nodes, the spline slopes where a table has no exact ones, and the derived numbers of the forms), with the energies held fixed. The rows of the line-of-sight tables are recomputed level by level for their transpose and are held to the forward’s row bit for bit, which the order of summation on a GPU does not promise; a row that differs is refused by name there, whereas on the CPU every row is served. At a \(\theta\) where the model is refused, the value is not a number and its gradient is zero.

## T:7.4 The likelihood

The log-likelihood of a model against data is a JAX function of the weights of the components and of the mass and length scales of the model, traceable and differentiable in both, and with the anisotropy of the named free components as parameters through the tangent rows above. The observables predicted by a model are read on the host once, as tables over projected radius; a projected radius in the units of the data is \(R = L\,l\,x\) and a speed is \(v = V(m/l)^{1/2}u\), with \(x\) and \(u\) in internal units, \(L\) and \(V\) the factors of the model’s units, and \(m\) and \(l\) the scales relative to the model’s own. For a superposed model, the composite profile for a new set of weights is one matrix-vector product over the members’ tabulated moments (Section T:6.9); the likelihood is linear in the weights up to their normalization, so its gradient in the weights is exact. A refused input inside the traced function (a negative weight, a radius outside the table) gives minus infinity with a zero gradient, never an exception, so that a sampler over the parameters always sees a value. A binned distribution holds the length scale at the model’s own value and carries no gradient in it, which a caller reads as not a number rather than as a number.

     On this page


---

# T:1 The model: density and potential

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/model

# T:1 The model: density and potential

## T:1.1 The two maps

The potential of the double power law and its expansions are given in Chiang+(2026d), Appendix A3, Eq. (A11), and Eq. (A13). Two consequences of those expansions are used below.

Near the center, \(P_0 - P \propto R^{2-\gamma}\,[1 + \mathcal{O}(R^{\alpha})]\). Since \(R^{\alpha} \propto (P_0-P)^{\delta}\), any function of \(R\) that is a series in \(R^{\alpha}\) is also a series in \((P_0 - P)^{\delta}\):

\begin{equation}
  R^{\alpha} \propto (P_0 - P)^{\delta}\left[1 + \mathcal{O}\!\left((P_0-P)^{\delta}\right)\right] .
  \tag{T:1.1}
\end{equation}
The coefficients of such a series are exact, and no fit is needed. The depth \(P_0 - P\) is itself a series in \(R^{\alpha}\) with known coefficients, Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (A11). Inverting that series order by order gives \(R = t\,[1 + S(t)]\), with \(t \propto (P_0-P)^{1/(2-\gamma)}\) and \(S\) a series in \(t^{\alpha}\). Substituting this inverse into the density and into the anisotropy factor of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) yields the coefficient of every power of \(P_0 - P\) as a finite sum of products of binomial coefficients. The package forms these coefficients in closed form by a power-series algebra, keeping every term up to three times the larger of \(\alpha\) and 2 beyond the leading power.

At large radii, the potential of an untruncated profile behaves as

\begin{equation}
  P \propto \begin{cases} R^{-1} & (\beta > 3),\\
   R^{-1}\ln R & (\beta = 3),\\
   R^{-(\beta-2)} & (2 < \beta < 3). \end{cases}
  \tag{T:1.2}
\end{equation}

## T:1.2 Derivatives of the auxiliary density

### T:1.2.1 The operator

The inversion requires \(\mathrm{d}^j\varrho_\mathrm{aux}/\mathrm{d} P^j\) up to \(j = m + 1\), and one order higher wherever the slope of the DF is tabulated as well. In Method I the profile is analytical and these derivatives are exact. The operator

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} P} = -\frac{R^2}{M(R)}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} R},
  \tag{T:1.3}
\end{equation}
with the closed-form enclosed mass \(M(R)\) of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (A7), is applied symbolically to the closed-form auxiliary density \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}(R) = \varrho(R)\,h(R)\), where \(h = R^{2\beta_\mathrm{c}}(1 \pm R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2)^{s}\) is the inverse of the anisotropy factor (\(s = 1\) for OM, \(s = 1 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\) for COM, and \(s = 0\) otherwise). The result is evaluated at \(R(P)\), which we obtain by bisection in \(\ln R\) on the monotonic \(P(R)\) and, near the center, on the subtraction-free depth. The potential \(P(R)\) itself never enters in closed form. A single expression of \(h\) serves every occurrence of the factor in the package: the Method I sources, the Method II sources, the edge law, the density of the Poisson solve, and the parameter derivatives of Section T:7. In Method II the input is a tabulated pair, and the derivatives are integrals of the parent’s DF (Section T:2.6).

Our first design for the tabulated case was a spline of \(\ln{\varrho_\mathrm{aux}}\) in \(P\) with knots placed by the equidistribution principle (de Boor 1978). Its derivatives of second and higher order carried the conditioning of the spline, which grows as the square of the ratio of its largest to its smallest knot spacing, into the inversion. The exact and integral forms replaced it.

### T:1.2.2 The inner series and where it is trusted

Near the center, the density, the enclosed mass, the depth, and the potential are the series of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (A9), Eq. (A12), and Eq. (A11), summed term by term with no subtraction from the central value. The series is trusted out to the largest radius at which its next term, relative to the depth, stays within one tenth of the goal. This bound follows from the parameters of the profile alone, and no fixed depth is assumed. The Poisson solve of a truncated model starts from the same series, and its inner rows are filled from the series out to that join (Section T:3.4).

## T:1.3 The profile of a truncated model

The self-consistent profile of a truncated model is a table of rows (radius, potential, density, and enclosed mass), and a single object owns its reading: every stage and every reader evaluates the profile through the four functions of that object and holds no interpolant of its own. The potential and the mass are cubic Hermite interpolants in the logarithms, with the exact slopes that the rows state, \(\mathrm{d}\ln P/\mathrm{d}\ln r = -M/(rP)\) and \(\mathrm{d}\ln M/\mathrm{d}\ln r = r^3\varrho/M\) (the Poisson equation and the mass integral). The density is a cubic spline of \(\ln\varrho\) in \(\ln r\), since the rows state no density slope. The radius at a given potential is the guarded inverse of the potential interpolant. A spatially finite profile carries its edge as its last row, where the density is zero and the radius is \(R_\mathrm{t}\). On the last interval the potential takes the Kepler form \(M_\mathrm{t}(1/r - 1/R_\mathrm{t})\) and the density follows the edge law \(\varrho_L\,(P/P_L)^{q}\), with the exponent \(q\) stated by the profile; beyond \(R_\mathrm{t}\) the potential is \(M_\mathrm{t}/r\) and the density is zero. Inside the first row, the interpolants continue as the power laws of the end rows. Nothing outside the domain is clipped: a radius that lies beyond the edge by a rounding error is treated as the edge, and anything further out is refused with a named reason.

     On this page


---

# T:6 Velocity profiles and projections

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/observables

# T:6 Velocity profiles and projections

An observable is a function of a model, and a request computes only what it needs. Two routes exist, and they share nothing but the model: the second moments follow from the density and the potential, whereas the velocity distributions follow from the DF, so each route checks the other. The prepared table of a model holds both routes and reads from them.

## T:6.1 Intrinsic moments

### T:6.1.1 The Jeans integral

For each component, the radial dispersion follows from the Jeans equation in the form

\begin{equation}
  \varrho_\mathrm{aux}\,\sigma_r^2\,(R) = \int_0^{P(R)} \varrho_\mathrm{aux}\,\mathrm{d} P ,
  \tag{T:6.1}
\end{equation}
with the member’s own \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\); the part of the integral below the lowest potential of the table is taken over the DF, and it is zero for a spatially finite model. The profile is tabulated in radius on rows from the first row of the profile to its last. Rows are added until every interval reads within the profile tolerance at its midpoint, and the nodes of the panels are doubled until \(\sigma_r\) moves by less than that tolerance. The superposition’s own route evaluates the integral on Gauss-Legendre nodes in \(\ln(1 - \mathcal{K}/P_0)\), which resolves the center, so that the two routes agree to rounding. The tangential dispersion of both tangential components together is \(\sigma_t^2 = 2(1 - \beta_\sigma)\,\sigma_r^2\), with \(\beta_\sigma\) the anisotropy of the model in closed form.

## T:6.2 Projection

The surface density and the line-of-sight dispersion, Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B46), come from a single line-of-sight rule with a single density, on two panels in the depth along the line of sight, at projected radii spaced logarithmically from the innermost row to a fixed fraction of the last row. Rows are added until the table reads itself between rows to within the tolerance of the certificate: the value read at a radius between two rows is compared with a row computed at that radius. Near a spatially finite edge, the table is read in \(x = \ln[R/(1 - R/R_\mathrm{t})]\), which is \(\ln R\) far inside and \(-\ln(1 - R/R_\mathrm{t})\) at the edge, so that the edge factor is resolved. A projected radius inside the innermost row is refused.

## T:6.3 Apertures

The dispersion inside an aperture is the surface-density weighted average of \(\sigma_{\rm los}^2\), Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B50). For an axisymmetric integrand every aperture reduces to a one-dimensional integral, \(\int f(R)\,\mathrm{arc}(R)\,R\,\mathrm{d} R\), where \(\mathrm{arc}(R)\) is the angular measure of the circle of radius \(R\) that lies inside the aperture. A centered circle takes nodes uniform in \(\ln R\) from the first row of the table. An offset circle has a full-circle core and a band of its own, the band under an end-point map in \(R - R_{\rm off}\) where it is narrow. A rectangle takes one panel between consecutive breaks of its arc, each with at least a stated number of Gauss-Legendre nodes and more per decade of its span. Above \(R_\mathrm{t}/\sqrt{2}\), where the factors \(R\) and \(v\) of the measure \(R\,\mathrm{d} R = -v\,\mathrm{d} v\) are equal, a panel is taken in \(v = (R_\mathrm{t}^2 - R^2)^{1/2}\), in which the integrand is smooth up to the edge. An aperture that encloses no tabulated surface density, or whose disk inside the first row carries more than a stated share of its weight, is refused with a named reason.

## T:6.4 The line-of-sight velocity distribution

The distribution \(D(R_{\rm 2D}, V)\) of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B53) is computed row by row at projected radii. On the plane \(V_{\rm los} = V\) at depth \(u\) along the line of sight, the level sets of \(Q\) are ellipses centered on the maximum of \(Q\), so the integral over the velocity plane is

\begin{equation}
  \iint F\,\mathrm{d} V_{\perp 1}\,\mathrm{d} V_{\perp 2} = \frac{R/R_{\rm 2D}}{\sqrt{Aq}}\int_0^{Q_c} F(Q_c - s)\,\Lambda(s)\,\mathrm{d} s ,
  \tag{T:6.2}
\end{equation}
with \(Q_c\) the maximum, \(Aq\) the product of the coefficients of the ellipse’s axes, and \(\Lambda(s)\) the integral of \((L^2)^{-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) around the level set. Where the DF carries no \(L\) factor, \(\Lambda = 2\pi\), and the \(s\) integral is the cumulative DF \(G(Q_c)\), read from a table of three branches. With the \(L\) factor, \(\Lambda = \int_0^{\pi}[(c_1 - c_2\cos\phi)^2 + c_3\sin^2\phi]^{-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,\mathrm{d}\phi\) is taken by a split rule that is dense toward the minimum of its base on each half, \(\phi = \lambda\sinh(\mu x)\) on \([0, \pi/2]\) with \(\mu = \mathrm{arsinh}(\pi/2\lambda)\), at a stated number of Gauss-Legendre nodes per half, as a JAX kernel; at \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = \pm 1/2\) it is a complete elliptic integral in closed form. The \(s\) integral is taken on Gauss-Legendre panels graded toward the energy of the DF’s floor, where the rule of the DF below its table meets the table. The point of zero angular momentum, where the non-analytic part of \(\Lambda\) behaves as \(|s - s_0|^{1-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\), and the point \(V = 0\), where \(\Lambda \propto s^{-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\), take graded layers whose count follows from \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) alone, namely the least count that integrates the end-point power to the tolerance, with a stated floor where a negative power is self-similar under the layers. The depth integral is taken on panels of each interval of the support along the line of sight, doubled until the tests of the row pass.

A row is taken on panels in \(V\), with breaks at the velocities where its layout changes: the velocity of the radial orbit, \(V_{\rm rad}\), and the velocity \(V_k\) at which the level set first meets the floor of the DF. Each is kept as a break only where the two panels adjacent to it carry more than a stated share of the row (decided once on the base rows, with each change bisected in \(\ln R_{\rm 2D}\)), with sub-panels graded toward zero velocity and toward each break at a stated ratio, and with the innermost sub-panel kept above the spacing of doubles at the break. Every row is normalized to one and checked against two quantities computed without it: its integral against the surface density, and its second moment against the projected dispersion (Section T:6.2).

A general-purpose integrator applied to the same integral, as in AGAMA (Vasiliev 2019), stops by default at a relative tolerance of \(10^{-3}\) for the moments and of \(10^{-2}\) for the distribution. The rows here are fixed rules whose every end-point behavior is removed by construction, and they are certified at the goal.

## T:6.5 The table of rows and its certificate

The base rows are placed at a stated number per decade of projected radius. By default they run from the first row of the profile out to the last base row beyond which the projected mass falls below the goal times the total projected mass; the rows that the profile would carry beyond that radius, where the DF is zero below the floor or the surface density is about zero, are not computed, and a read beyond the last row, including a read at a single point, is refused with the radius of the last row and the setting that moves it named. The inner end is kept at full depth by default. A user who will read the table only outside a stated projected radius may give that radius, and the rows then start where the projected mass inside the first row falls below the goal times the projected mass inside the stated radius; a read inside the first row is refused in the same words. Rows are added toward each radius where the layout changes, toward the end, and wherever a stretch is short. Rows are then added until the distribution read between two neighboring rows, by a stencil of a stated number of rows, agrees with a row computed there to the tolerance of the settings. An interval that cannot be closed is recorded with its reason, and a request inside it is refused with that reason named. The certificate of the table is its last estimate of its reading between rows, in units of its tolerances. The rows are computed in a pool of processes, one row per process. The report of the table (Section T:8.1) carries the worst norm and second moment over the rows, the rows that could not be judged, the rows whose depth rule did not converge, the certificate, and the floor of the layers at the point of zero angular momentum where \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) lies between \(1/2\) and \(1\).

## T:6.6 The distribution in an aperture

The distribution inside an aperture is the surface-density weighted average of the rows over the aperture, that is, the form of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B77) for one component. No row is computed for it. The rows are read at the radii of the aperture’s rule (Section T:6.3), with every break of a row followed as a function of radius, and each radius is scanned once. The result is formed on its own panels in \(V\), with breaks at zero, at the smallest and the largest value of each row break over the aperture, and at the top; a velocity that meets a break curve inside the aperture takes the radii where the curve equals it as breaks of its radial rule. The output rule refines itself by bisecting its widest sub-panels until its norm and its second moment are within one hundredth of the goal of the rows’ own rule. At any velocity, the distribution is the polynomial of its panel through the panel’s own nodes, namely the Legendre series of the antiderivative of the quadrature, so that it integrates exactly as the quadrature does. Its second moment is checked against the dispersion of the aperture from the projected tables, which reads no distribution.

## T:6.7 Gauss-Hermite moments

With \(y = (V - V_*)/\sigma_*\), where \(V_*\) and \(\sigma_*\) are the mean and the dispersion of the distribution itself, the moments of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B63) are

\begin{equation}
  h_n = 2\sqrt{\pi}\int D(V)\,H_n(y)\,\frac{e^{-y^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\mathrm{d} V , \qquad H_3 = \frac{2y^3 - 3y}{\sqrt{3}}, \quad H_4 = \frac{4y^4 - 12y^2 + 3}{2\sqrt{6}} ,
  \tag{T:6.3}
\end{equation}
with the Hermite functions of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B61). They are taken on the velocity nodes and weights of a row or of an aperture distribution, mirrored to both signs and normalized to unit integral. The standardized moments by direct sums are reported beside them; to first order, \(s_3 = 4\sqrt{3}\,h_3\) and \(s_4 = 3 + 8\sqrt{6}\,h_4\). Moments at projected radii are tabulated once over radius and read between rows; moments over apertures are taken on the distribution of each aperture.

## T:6.8 The local speed distribution

With \(t = \cos\eta\), where \(\eta\) is the angle between the velocity and the radius, \(\xi = (r/R_\mathrm{a})^2\), and \(s\) the sign of the anisotropy (\(+1\) for Type I, \(-1\) for Type II, and \(0\) without \(R_\mathrm{a}\)),

\begin{equation}
  p(V\,|\,r) = \frac{4\pi}{\varrho(r)}\,r^{-2b}\,V^{2-2b}\int_0^{1}(1 - t^2)^{-b}\,F(Q)\,\mathrm{d} t , \qquad Q = P(r) - \frac{V^2}{2}(1 + s\xi) + \frac{s\xi V^2}{2}\,t^2 ,
  \tag{T:6.4}
\end{equation}
where \(b\) is \(\beta_\mathrm{c}\) for the constant and COM classes and 0 otherwise. Since \(Q\) is quadratic in \(t\), the edge of the support of the DF is an end of the interval in \(t\) and never an interior point. The interval is split where \(Q\) crosses the first energy of the table, and for \(b > 0\) the piece that ends at \(t = 1\) is integrated in \(w\), with \(1 - t = w^{p}\) and \(p = 1/(1 - b)\), so that \((1 - t)^{-b}\,\mathrm{d} t = p\,\mathrm{d} w\). A Type II model holds orbits of negative energy, and its speeds reach \(V_{\rm esc}/\sqrt{1 - r^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2}\); the share beyond the escape speed is reported. Each radius is computed with three checks: the norm against the density, the second moment against \(\sigma_r^2(3 - 2\beta_\sigma)\), and the change of the distribution when the nodes of its angle rule are doubled, at most three times, until that change falls below the tolerance.

## T:6.9 Superposed models

A superposed model (Section T:4) is projected one component at a time, each on its own tables, and the components are then combined with their weights. The members share one surface density, so the projected second moment is linear in the weights,

\begin{equation}
  \sigma_{\rm los}^2(R) = \sum_i c_i\,\sigma_{{\rm los},i}^2(R) ,
  \tag{T:6.5}
\end{equation}
and the same holds for the intrinsic second moments. With the projected moments of each member tabulated once, the composite profile for a new set of weights costs one matrix-vector product, which is what the likelihood of Section T:7.4 evaluates. A distribution at a projected radius mixes by the surface densities, \(D = \sum_k w_k\Sigma_k D_k/\sum_k w_k\Sigma_k\); a distribution in an aperture mixes by the projected masses inside it; and the local speed distribution mixes by the densities at that radius.

     On this page


---

# T:0 Principles and conventions

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/principles

# T:0 Principles and conventions

## T:0.1 Notation

We adopt the notation of Chiang+(2026d). The relative potential is \(P\), with the central value \(P_0\); the energy-like variable is \(\mathcal{K}\); the distribution function (DF) is \(F(\mathcal{K}, L) = F_\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{K})\,L^{-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\); the density is the double power law of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (5) with exponents \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\); and \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) is the auxiliary density, which for the (C)OM models is given by Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B24). Three derived quantities are used throughout these notes. The first is the order of the inversion,

\begin{equation}
  \nu \equiv \tfrac{3}{2} - \beta_\mathrm{c} = m + n, \qquad m \equiv \lfloor \nu \rfloor, \qquad 0 \leq n < 1 ,
  \tag{T:0.1}
\end{equation}
and the other two are the exponent of the inner expansion and the depth below the center,

\begin{equation}
  \delta \equiv \frac{\alpha}{2-\gamma}, \qquad u \equiv P_0 - \mathcal{K} .
  \tag{T:0.2}
\end{equation}
Internally, every model is expressed in the units of Chiang+(2026d), in which the scale radius and the central potential of the untruncated profile are both unity; a truncated model therefore has \(P_0 = 1 - \mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\). The depth \(u\) is carried as a variable of its own wherever the difference \(P_0 - \mathcal{K}\) would lose significant digits.

## T:0.2 Rules derived from the inputs, not fitted constants

Every numerical choice in the package is either a function of its inputs (the model and the settings tier) or a property of the host arithmetic; none is a fitted constant. Wherever a threshold appears, it is derived from the problem at hand. For example, the depth at which a table ends is the depth at which the exact derivatives leave the range of a double (Section T:2.5.2); the radius out to which the inner series is trusted is the radius at which its next term reaches the tolerance (Section T:1.2.2); and the radius of trust of an untruncated product follows from the offset of the solver (Section T:3.7). A settings tier changes only node counts and tolerances, and a runtime option (verbosity, timing, workers, device) changes no number at all. Whatever cannot be computed is refused with a named reason, and the object computed so far is returned as the result of the error; nothing is silently approximated.

## T:0.3 Exact arithmetic

Wherever a quantity has a closed form, we use that closed form, and we form its derivatives symbolically rather than by finite differences. The derivatives of the auxiliary density with respect to the potential are built by computer algebra from the closed-form density, enclosed mass, and anisotropy factor (Section T:1.2.1). They are evaluated in double precision where that evaluation is stable, and in arbitrary precision where it suffers from cancellation: at small and at large radii, at high orders far out, and within a band around \(R_\mathrm{a}\) for a Type II model. The coefficients of the central series of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) are exact (Section T:2.2.1); the amplitude of the central term of the DF is a closed form; and the enclosed mass is the incomplete Beta function, evaluated in arbitrary precision where its closed form fails. Every exact form is certified against an arbitrary-precision reference in the test suite (Section T:8).

## T:0.4 Host floors

Three limits of double precision shape every table, and all three are read from the host rather than assumed. The energy grid has a floor at \(q_0 = 10^{-10}\) in units of \(P_0\), and it ends at a gap of \(10^{-9}\) below \(P_0\), which is the depth at which energies are still separable from the center; no node lies above this gap, and the closed form of the center carries the DF beyond the last node (Section T:2.5.2). The top of a table may end deeper still, at the shallower of two depths: the depth at which the exact derivatives needed by the inversion exceed the largest double, and the depth at the smallest radius whose square the host can represent (\(2^{-537}\) with subnormals). Both depths are computed from the model alone. Near the center, the depth is formed without subtraction, from the inner series (Section T:1.2.2) and, in the lookup, from node differences that are exact by Sterbenz’s lemma (Section T:2.5.4).

## T:0.5 Accuracy tiers, reports, and refusals

Every product is judged against three levels of relative error: a goal of \(10^{-6}\), a ceiling of \(10^{-4}\), and a hard limit of \(10^{-2}\). A check within the goal is silent. A check above the goal is returned with a warning that stays attached to the result and to everything computed from it. A check beyond the hard limit refuses the result, unless the settings explicitly ask for it. Every result carries a report with a fixed set of checks (Section T:8.1); a derived result holds its own checks together with the worst tier of its parents, never a copy of their reports. A component of a product that feeds a projected quantity is held to one tenth of the goal, which is its share of the error budget of what is computed from it.

Two settings tiers are tested, the default tier and a quick tier for exploration. Both are held to the same checks by the test suite, and the quick tier changes only node counts. The CPU-only mode gives the same numbers on every machine, and every file records the backend that produced it. A stage whose wall time scales with a sequential count (the steps of a solve, or rows computed one at a time) is latency-bound on a GPU, and it therefore stays on the CPU on every device; a stage whose wall time scales with a batch (the speed table, the particle draw) runs on a GPU when one is present. The rows of the line-of-sight tables are computed in a pool of CPU processes, one row per process, and never reach a GPU. This classification rests on measured scaling, with no margin constant.

     On this page


---
