# T:5 Particle sampling

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sampling

# T:5 Particle sampling

## T:5.1 The velocity distribution at a given radius factorizes

At radius \(R\), let \(V\) be the speed and \(\varphi\) the angle between the velocity and the radial direction, so that \(L = R\,V\sin\varphi\). For the (C)OM models, the argument of the DF is

\begin{equation}
  Q_\mp = P - \tfrac{1}{2}\,f\,V^2, \qquad f(R, \varphi) \equiv 1 \pm \frac{R^2}{R_\mathrm{a}^2}\sin^2\varphi ,
  \tag{T:5.1}
\end{equation}
with the upper sign for Type I and the lower sign for Type II; \(f = 1\) for constant anisotropy. The probability density of \((V, \varphi)\) at \(R\), Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B40), is \(\propto V^{2-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\sin^{1-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\!\varphi\;F_\mathcal{K}(P - \tfrac12 f V^2)\). In the variable

\begin{equation}
  x \equiv V\sqrt{\frac{f}{2P}} \in [0, 1]
  \tag{T:5.2}
\end{equation}
it becomes a product,

\begin{equation}
  p(x, \varphi\,|\,R) \propto \underbrace{\sin^{1-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\!\varphi\; f^{-\nu}}_{p(\varphi|R)} \;\times\; \underbrace{x^{2-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,F_\mathcal{K}\!\left[P\,(1-x^2)\right]}_{p(x|P)} .
  \tag{T:5.3}
\end{equation}
Three consequences follow.

The angle and the scaled speed are independent, and each can be drawn from a one-dimensional distribution.

The distribution of \(x\) depends on the radius only through \(P(R)\) and is the same for every \(\varphi\); the speed is \(V = x\sqrt{2P/f}\).

The distribution of the angle is known in closed form. For Type I at \(R > R_\mathrm{a}\), it turns over at \(\sin\varphi_{\rm c} = R_\mathrm{a}/R\), the angle at which \(f = 2\); the orbits become radial over an angular scale that shrinks as \(R_\mathrm{a}/R\).

## T:5.2 The table of speeds

### T:5.2.1 The rows

By Eq. (T:5.3), the scaled speed \(x\) has a distribution that depends on \(P\) alone. One table therefore serves the whole model. Its rows are indexed by the potential, uniform in \(\ln[P/(P_0 - P)]\) over the range of the profile with one guard row beyond each end, and no grid in radius or in angle is needed. Each row stores the inverse of the cumulative distribution \(\mathcal{U}(x)\) in logit variables,

\begin{equation}
  s = \ln\frac{x}{x_{\rm e} - x} \quad\text{against}\quad \lambda_{\mathcal{U}} = \ln\frac{\mathcal{U}}{1-\mathcal{U}} ,
  \tag{T:5.4}
\end{equation}
where \(x_{\rm e} \leq 1\) is the edge of the support of \(x\) on that row. Both ends of the distribution are power laws, so \(s\) is close to linear in \(\lambda_{\mathcal{U}}\) toward either end, and one table per row covers the whole range of \(\mathcal{U}\). The table carries its exact slope,

\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d} s}{\mathrm{d}\lambda_{\mathcal{U}}} = \frac{x_{\rm e}\,\mathcal{U}\,(1-\mathcal{U})}{p(x|P)\,x\,(x_{\rm e}-x)} ,
  \tag{T:5.5}
\end{equation}
with \(p(x|P)\) normalized on the row, and it is read by cubic Hermite interpolation. Between two rows, \(s\) is interpolated by a cubic Hermite in the row variable, with the exact slope across rows at fixed \(\mathcal{U}\) stored as a third channel. A particle at radius \(R\) and angle \(\varphi\) takes \(x\) at \(P(R)\) and the speed \(V = x\sqrt{2P/f}\) of Eq. (T:5.2); nothing is inverted when a particle is drawn.

A row is built from the mass of the density on the panels of a velocity grid, refined at both ends by Gauss-Legendre panels in the logarithm of \(x\) and of \(x_{\rm e} - x\), with the closed forms of the power laws beyond. The cumulative masses from each end at the edges of the panels are the construction nodes; their cubic Hermite is inverted at the nodes of the table, and each node is polished by a safeguarded Newton step on the true residual. The rows are refined, with every row kept, until the table’s own error across rows falls below the goal or the row count reaches its cap; the report carries that error, and a table beyond the hard limit is refused. Our first design was a two-dimensional grid of the cumulative distribution in \((\ln R, V/V_\mathrm{esc})\), read by bilinear interpolation. The factorization of Eq. (T:5.3) removes the radius from the table, and the logit variables resolve both ends of each row.

### T:5.2.2 The radius and the angle

The radius is drawn from the inverse of the enclosed-mass fraction \(\mathcal{U} = M(R)/M(R_{\rm e})\), tabulated in the same logit variables with \(R\) in place of \(x\) and the outer radius of the sampling, \(R_{\rm e}\), in place of \(x_{\rm e}\). Its slope follows from \(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{U}/\mathrm{d} R = 4\pi R^2\varrho/M(R_{\rm e})\), which is exact everywhere, and the mass fraction is exact at the rows of the profile. The variables are power laws at both ends whether the edge is smooth (the truncation radius) or sharp (a radius given by the user); at a sharp edge the last interval is refined at halved distances from the edge. The angle of an anisotropic model needs no table in radius. By Eq. (T:5.3), \(p(\varphi|R) \propto \sin^{1-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\!\varphi\,f^{-\nu}\), and the substitution

\begin{equation}
  \sin^2\varphi = \frac{y}{1 \pm \xi\,(1-y)}, \qquad \xi \equiv \frac{R^2}{R_\mathrm{a}^2},
  \tag{T:5.6}
\end{equation}
with the upper sign for Type I and the lower sign for Type II, turns it into a Beta distribution of \(y\) with parameters \((1-\beta_\mathrm{c},\,1/2)\) at every radius. One inverse table of that variate serves the whole model, each half tabulated against the logarithm of the probability at its own end, with the slope \(u/[y\,p(y)]\) in closed form. The angle is drawn in \([0, \pi/2]\), and the sign of the radial velocity is drawn independently; the direction of the tangential component is a Gram-Schmidt projection of an independent isotropic Gaussian draw onto the plane perpendicular to the radius.

## T:5.3 The draw

Every variable is drawn by inversion, and nothing is rejected. The random numbers of particle \(i\) depend only on the seed, the component, and \(i\): its key is folded from the seed and the component and then from \(i\), and each variable takes its own channel of that key. The first \(n\) particles of a larger draw are therefore the same particles, on every machine and backend and for any block size. The potential at a particle is the profile’s own (Section T:1.3), never a linear interpolation on a table. A draw is made in blocks of a stated size, so that its working memory is that of one block, whatever the total count. The particles of a superposed model (Section T:4) are drawn through the enclosed mass of the mixture, with each component’s share of the particles.

A draw bounded to a range of radii takes the uniform variate between the mass fractions of the two radii, so that every particle lands in the range and the particles carry the mass of the range. A speed drawn in a window at a radius takes the variate between the table’s own values at the ends of the window, for a constant anisotropy, where the window does not couple to the angle. A projected pair sampler draws \((R_{\rm 2D}, V_{\rm los})\) on an annulus and in a window of velocity from the cumulative surface density and the line-of-sight tables (Section T:6.5), exactly conditioned.

## T:5.4 What a draw checks

Every particle must lie inside the phase-space support of the DF of its component. The bound is checked on the draw’s own variables, the scaled speed and its distance from the edge of the support, which hold it exactly; the velocity is then checked against the bound from which it was built, \(V^2 + \sigma\,\xi\,V_t^2 \leq 2\Psi\) with \(\xi = (r/R_\mathrm{a})^2\) (zero for a constant anisotropy), to within a stated multiple of its own rounding floor. A particle that fails either check is refused. Every writer reads its file back and compares it with what it wrote, bit for bit after the cast to the type of the file.

     On this page


---

# T:4 Superposition

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/sup

# T:4 Superposition

Distribution functions inverted from one and the same truncated density, that is, Method II children of one parent, combined with positive weights that sum to one, form a single equilibrium model in that density. Members on different truncated profiles are refused, and every component keeps its own energy grid, certified on its own nodes. The anisotropy profile of the superposition is given in Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B74). In terms of the radial dispersions \(\sigma_{r,i}^2\) and the anisotropy profiles \(\beta_i\) of the members, with weights \(c_i > 0\) and \(\sum_i c_i = 1\), it reads

\begin{equation}
  \beta_{\rm sup}(R) = \frac{\sum_i c_i\,\beta_i(R)\,\sigma_{r,i}^2(R)}{\sum_i c_i\,\sigma_{r,i}^2(R)} .
  \tag{T:4.1}
\end{equation}
The range of anisotropy profiles that a superposition can reach is set by three limits.

Outer value. At the truncation radius,

\begin{equation}
  \beta_{\rm sup}(R_\mathrm{t}) = \sum_i c_i\,\beta_i(R_\mathrm{t}),
  \tag{T:4.2}
\end{equation}
which is a single linear constraint on the weights. In practice this is the limit that binds.

Central value. \(\beta_{\rm sup}(0)\) equals the largest positive central anisotropy among the members in use; if all central anisotropies are negative, it is the weighted harmonic mean of their central values.

Transition. The (C)OM profiles change over about one decade in radius. A target profile that changes over a wider range is approached by mixing members with different anisotropy radii.

The composite dispersions are computed from Eq. (T:4.1) and the Jeans integral of Section T:6.1.1 without any sampling. Downstream of this section, a superposition is treated as one model: its particles are drawn through the enclosed mass of the mixture with each component’s share (Section T:5.3), its projected observables are formed one component at a time and mixed by the weights (Section T:6.9), and its likelihood is linear in the weights (Section T:7.4).


---

# T:3 Truncation

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/truncation

# T:3 Truncation

The two truncation methods are defined in Chiang+(2026d), Section 3.1.

## T:3.1 Type II models beyond the anisotropy radius

The model is not defined for \(R > R_\mathrm{a}\). In the Type II variable \(Q_+\), the tangential velocity enters with the factor \(1 - R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2\). For \(R > R_\mathrm{a}\) this factor is negative, the velocity integral diverges, and no DF of this form yields a density. An untruncated profile that extends beyond \(R_\mathrm{a}\) therefore has no Type II DF, whereas a truncated model with \(R_\mathrm{t} \leq {R_\mathrm{a}}\) is well defined.

Method I nevertheless needs \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) there. The inversion solves the Volterra equation Eq. (T:2.3), whose lower limit lies at \(R = \infty\). The values of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) on \(P > P(R_\mathrm{a})\) determine \(F_\mathcal{K}\) there only in combination with \(F_\mathcal{K}\) on \(P < P(R_\mathrm{a})\). Method I constructs the truncated DF from the untruncated one by the shift of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B27), and the contribution of the stretch \(0 < P < P(R_\mathrm{a})\) to \(F_\mathcal{K}\) depends on \(\mathcal{K}\), so it does not cancel in that difference. A value of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) must therefore be supplied on that stretch.

The continuation. For OM Type II, the factor \(1 - R^2/R_\mathrm{a}^2\) is a polynomial and is used as it stands. For COM Type II with non-integer \(1 - \beta_\mathrm{c}\), the factor \(w^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) is not real for \(w < 0\). PIANISTpy adopts the continuation

\begin{equation}
  w^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}} \;\to\; \mathrm{sign}(w)\,|w|^{1-\beta_\mathrm{c}},
  \tag{T:3.1}
\end{equation}
which is odd in \(w\) and reduces to the OM form at \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 0\). The continuation is requested through an explicit argument in the symbolic form of the Method I inversion alone; every other reading of the factor at or beyond \(R_\mathrm{a}\) is refused with a named reason. The adopted convention is recorded in the product file.

The support. An untruncated Type II model is defined only inside \(R_\mathrm{a}\), so its DF is returned over \(\mathcal{K} > P(R_\mathrm{a})\) only. The table keeps its fixed grid, the rows at and below \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) hold no value, and the record states the first row of the support. The values that the inversion forms below \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) belong to the continuation rather than to the model, whatever their sign; they are used by the inversion above \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\), which depends on them non-locally, and they are not reported. The gates on the sign and on the last minimum of \(F_\mathcal{K}\) are evaluated on the support, and the lowest admissible truncation value is \(\max(\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_{\min}, P(R_\mathrm{a}))\), so that every truncated Type II model has \(R_\mathrm{t} < R_\mathrm{a}\). The anisotropy object declares the edge of its domain (\(R_\mathrm{a}\) for Type II, none otherwise), and no rule reads the Type directly. The same bound holds for a Method II child whose anisotropy is of Type II: its \(R_\mathrm{a}\) lies beyond the parent’s edge by the existence condition.

What the convention can and cannot change. Every DF of the form \(\hat F(\hat{\mathcal{K}})\,L^{-2\beta_\mathrm{c}}\) in the Type II variable has the COM Type II anisotropy profile, and the truncated density is computed from \(\hat F\). The convention therefore affects neither the anisotropy profile nor the self-consistency of a Method I model. What it selects is which truncated density the model has, and under Method I that density is an output. For that density the DF is unique. The effect of the convention on the truncated density exceeds the accuracy goal of Section T:0.5.

Method II inverts the truncated pair, which lies within \(R_\mathrm{a}\), and never evaluates the continuation. A user who needs a Type II model with a prescribed density should therefore use Method II.

## T:3.2 The truncated DF and the Poisson source

From the table that the inversion leaves, the truncation energy, and the settings, the truncated DF \(F(\mathcal{K} + \mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}) - F(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t})\) is formed on the source grid, together with its Taylor form at the edge and the edge integral that joins the form to the table. The auxiliary density

\begin{equation}
  \varrho_\mathrm{aux}(P) = \int_0^{P} \hat F(\mathcal{K})\,\left[2(P - \mathcal{K})\right]^{n}\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{K}
  \tag{T:3.2}
\end{equation}
is what the Poisson solve takes as its source; the density of a component is \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) multiplied by the factor of its anisotropy in \(r\), which the solve applies. The source grid runs from the floor to the gap below the truncated central potential, with logarithmic tails toward both ends over a stated fraction of the top. The integral at each potential is taken on two intervals: nodes uniform in \(\ln{\mathcal{K}}\) below a split at a stated fraction of \(P\), and above the split the map \(\mathcal{K} = P - v^{k}\), which removes the end-point behavior of the kernel where \(n\) is not negative. The lookup at a grid node returns the node’s value; no clip by an absolute epsilon enters a quantity that spans ten decades, and the rows below the floor are zero by the DF’s own rule.

### T:3.2.1 The tail of the DF in the density integral

For an untruncated model whose DF has the tail of Eq. (T:2.13), the lower sub-interval is evaluated as

\begin{equation}
  F_\mathcal{K} = A\,\mathcal{K}^{-a} + F_\mathcal{K}^{\rm smooth},
  \tag{T:3.3}
\end{equation}
with the power law integrated in closed form by Eq. (T:2.14) and the remainder integrated numerically. In Method I, the part of the integral below the floor uses the exact stretch of Section T:2.3.2 rather than the power law. A truncated DF has no such tail, and the term is absent.

## T:3.3 The Poisson solve

The truncated Poisson equation, Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B28), is integrated outward in \(s = \ln r\) as a first-order system in \([\Phi,\; W = r\,\mathrm{d}\Phi/\mathrm{d} r,\; u = P_0 - \Phi]\), under relative and absolute tolerances of \(10^{-11}\), starting from the series of the cusp (Section T:1.2.2). The right-hand side is the density of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B29), read from the source table of Section T:3.2. The solve ends at the event where \(\Phi\) reaches the floor, which is the edge of a spatially finite model, or else at the outer radius; the last rows of a truncated model are re-solved on a grid geometric in \(R_\mathrm{t} - r\), and the row at the floor is the crossing of the event. A request whose solve reaches no edge within its radius is refused with a named reason. The solve is a serial integration, and it runs on the CPU on every device (Section T:0.5).

## T:3.4 The fills and the rows of the profile

The rows of the solve are sparse where the potential approaches the floor and where it approaches the center, so both ends are filled to the row density of the profile: at least a stated number of rows per decade of the potential and of the depth, in bins of a stated width, over the profile’s own span. The inner end is the inner series of Section T:1.2.2, lowered by the central deficit where the model carries one, out to the join where the series and the rows of the solve agree; between the join and the threshold of the fill, the solve’s own interpolant is used. The outer end is a log-log interpolation of the solve’s rows in the potential, continued below its lowest rows by their own slope and, below the Taylor switch, by the closed form of the edge. The rows that the profile keeps are those which the solve reached reliably, from the innermost radius requested to the last row at or above the floor; a profile that reaches no edge is read to its last row.

## T:3.5 The gates on the truncation energy

The truncation of Chiang+(2026d), Eq. (B27) requires a DF that is non-negative and non-decreasing above the truncation energy. From the computed untruncated DF, the code takes the highest zero crossing and the position of the last minimum, and it accepts a truncation energy only above the larger of the two and, for a Type II model, strictly above \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) (Section T:3.1). The bound at \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\) is necessary but not sufficient: only the truncated solve places the edge, and a solve whose edge lies at or beyond \(R_\mathrm{a}\) is refused by the same name afterward. A truncation that no model can carry is refused before any stage runs: a cusp shallower than \(2\beta_\mathrm{c}(0)\) at the center, where the DF is negative there for every truncation (An & Evans 2006); a degenerate central series (Section T:2.5.1); and a central DF that tends to a negative value.

## T:3.6 A target mass or a target radius

Under Method I the untruncated DF does not depend on the truncation, so it is inverted once, and every evaluation of a target costs one truncated solve. The search runs on \(x = \ln{\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}}\) for a target \(v = M_\mathrm{t}\) or \(v = R_\mathrm{t}\), in four stages: deeper truncation from a probe until the model is admissible; a bracket by secant steps in \((\ln{\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}}, \ln v)\) toward the target, by at most a factor of 16 per step, until one admissible model lies on each side; where a step lands outside the admissible set, its boundary, namely the \(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\) at which \(R_\mathrm{t}\) reaches its limit (the cap, or \(R_\mathrm{a}\)), found by regula falsi on \(1/R_\mathrm{t}\); and finally the Illinois form of regula falsi on \((\ln{\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}}, \ln(v/\text{target}))\) until \(|v/\text{target} - 1|\) is within the goal. A value of \(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\) is admissible when its solve succeeds, the model is spatially finite, \(R_\mathrm{t}\) is within the cap and, for Type II, inside \(R_\mathrm{a}\), and \(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\) lies at or above the gates and at or below \(0.9\) of the central potential; on the admissible set both targets decrease with \(\mathcal{K}_\mathrm{t}\). When no admissible model reaches the target, the request is refused with a named reason and the value reached at the limit that binds; the solve takes no fallback.

## T:3.7 The radius of trust of an untruncated product

The solution without truncation must recover \(P \to 0\) as \(R \to \infty\). In practice it differs from the exact potential at large radii by a small constant \(\epsilon\), its integration constant, which we measure against the potential of the source profile beyond \(R = 10^3\). A constant offset in \(P\) changes the potential and the density by

\begin{equation}
  \left|\frac{\delta P}{P}\right| = \frac{|\epsilon|}{P}, \qquad \left|\frac{\delta\varrho}{\varrho}\right| = \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln\varrho}{\mathrm{d}\ln P}\right|\frac{|\epsilon|}{P},
  \tag{T:3.4}
\end{equation}
both of which grow outward. The radius of trust \(R_{\rm trust}(g)\) is the largest radius at which both stay below a relative accuracy \(g\). It is recorded in the product for several values of \(g\) between the goal and the ceiling of Section T:0.5, and untruncated tables are cut at \(R_{\rm trust}(10^{-4})\) by default. Beyond the radius where the potential has fallen to half its central value, the rows of an untruncated model are the closed forms of the source profile on a fixed logarithmic grid, out to the radius where \(P\) reaches the floor, so that the end of the table does not move with the offset. Truncated products are not cut.

## T:3.8 What a model checks

Each check is read on the rows of the profile through the profile object of Section T:1.3, so a model from a run and a model from a file are checked alike. The Poisson residual is Poisson’s equation in integral form on every interval between consecutive rows, including the edge row, \(\Phi(r_a) - \Phi(r_b) = \int M/r^2\,\mathrm{d} r\) and \(M(r_b) - M(r_a) = \int \varrho\,r^2\,\mathrm{d} r\), each relative to the larger of its two rows. The round trip compares the density that the model’s own DF gives at a row, \(\varrho = C(\beta_\mathrm{c})\int_0^{\Phi} F(Q)\,[2(\Phi - Q)]^{1/2-\beta_\mathrm{c}}\,\mathrm{d} Q\) divided by the anisotropy’s factor in \(r\), with \(F\) read through the lookup, against the density of the row. It is evaluated at the rows nearest to each half-decade of radius and at every row from the last of those to the edge, so that the check reads what a dense read would read. The row density is the count of rows per bin that the fills keep; it is silent where every bin is full and refused at any shortfall.

     On this page


---

# T:8 Verification

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/reference/technical-notes/verification

# T:8 Verification

## T:8.1 Reports and tiers

Every result carries a validation report with a fixed set of keys for its kind, one check per key, with its relative error and, where applicable, the radius or energy at which it is worst. The report is not a log: nothing is appended to it, and a derived result holds its own checks together with the worst tier of its parents. The checks are the following. For a DF: the slope column, the center against the top decade, the joins below the floor, the sign report, and the validity certificate (Section T:2.5.5). For a model: the Poisson residual, the round trip, and the row density (Section T:3.8), with the radii of trust of an untruncated result. For a line-of-sight table: the norm, the second moment, the unjudged rows, the convergence of the depth rule, the certificate, and the layer floor (Section T:6.5). For an aperture distribution: its norm by its own weights and its second moment against the dispersion of the aperture. For the local speed distribution: its norm, its second moment, and its change under doubling. For a draw: the bound on the support. Each tier is read as in Section T:0.5.

## T:8.2 Reference values

The exact forms are certified against references that owe nothing to the numerical pipeline. The symbolic derivatives of \(\varrho_\mathrm{aux}\) are compared with quadrature and differentiation in arbitrary precision at thirty digits; the derivatives of the anisotropy factor with the symbolic third derivative of its expression evaluated in arbitrary precision; the central series at the anchor with the symbolic derivatives of the closed-form density; and the closed-form DFs of the isotropic Hernquist and Plummer models, and of the NFW profile at \(\beta_\mathrm{c} = 1/2\) (Section T:2.2.5), with the table of the inversion. The two routes to every projected quantity (Section T:6) are held to the goal against each other, and a run of the full pipeline is compared bit for bit with the stored products that it reproduces on the same backend; every file is read back and compared with what was written.

## T:8.3 The roundtrip test

The test of Chiang+(2026d), Section 4, shown in Chiang+(2026d), Fig. 8, starts from the untruncated isotropic NFW profile, computes the DF, integrates it to a density, and solves the Poisson equation with \(P(0) = 1\). Every curve is numerical, and the only analytical quantity is the target density.

PIANISTpy. The standard untruncated isotropic product: the inverted DF, the velocity quadrature, and a numerical Poisson solve.

AGAMA. All defaults: the multipole potential built from the density on its default grid with the radial extent detected automatically, the default isotropic quasi-spherical DF with the exact action finder, and the density from its moments routine.

galpy. Its interpolated spherical potential on a grid denser and wider than its default, and its Eddington DF with every default. Its DF is zero beyond the default outer radius of that routine. galpy has no Poisson solver and therefore no density curve.

Fitting functions. Passed through the same velocity quadrature and Poisson solve as the PIANISTpy DF.

The numbers behind the figure are reproduced by the notebooks that accompany these notes.

## T:8.4 The accuracy grid

A fixed set of models, four tables of rows by columns over the exponents of the profile and the anisotropy models, is run unchanged at every release at both settings tiers. The DF of each model is inverted, its density is computed back from it, and the roundtrip error is read on a dense grid of radii. Each cell records the maximum and the median over the stated range, the tier that the result itself reports, or the name of the refusal where the package refuses the model; the grid states for every cell the outcome it expects, so that a release is compared with the last one cell by cell. A Type II model without a truncation has its DF only above \(P(R_\mathrm{a})\), and its cell gives the tier that the package reports over that support. The tables are published with the documentation; the measured values live there and in the notebooks, not in these notes.

     On this page

# Install

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/install

# Install

```
pip install pianistpy

```

PIANISTpy needs Python 3.11 or later and runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.

The test suite is installed with the package. To run it on an installation:

```
pip install "pianistpy[test]"
pytest --pyargs pianistpy

```

## Dependencies

The dependencies are installed by pip with the package. Two lists are kept with every release: the versions the
release was developed and tested with, and the oldest versions of the listed dependencies that pass the full test
suite together.

Package

Standard (tested with)

Minimum (oldest that passes the suite)

Python

3.11

3.11 (the oldest NumPy 2.3 supports)

2.4

1.17

1.14

0.7.2

0.7.1

Optimistix

0.1.0

0.1.0

Astropy below 7.2 needs NumPy below 2.4 (older Astropy calls a function NumPy 2.4 removed).

This standard list is the systematically tested environment, which can differ from the default package versions
that pip installs by taking the newest version of each dependency that PIANISTpy allows. To reproduce the tested
environment, manual specifications of each dependent package version during installation may be required. JAX
0.10.2 and later are not allowed by PIANISTpy, because one test of the suite fails on 0.10.2.

## CPU and GPU

PIANISTpy runs on the CPU with the default installation. With a CUDA build of JAX installed, it automatically
becomes GPU-enabled for the GPU-implemented features, with no manual setting needed in PIANISTpy. JAX’s CUDA builds
are for Linux only, so macOS runs the CPU-only mode. A native Windows Python also runs the CPU-only mode; on
Windows the GPU is reached through the Windows Subsystem for Linux (or a Linux virtual machine). Results on the
GPU and the CPU agree to better than \(10^{-10}\) in relative terms, and the accuracy goal holds on both. To
choose the CPU or the GPU explicitly, see Runtime options.

In ver. 1.0.0, only the particle sampler (its speed table and the draw) uses the GPU.

     On this page


---

# What PIANISTpy does

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/overview

# What PIANISTpy does

Density profiles. Analytical double-power-law density profiles with a finite central
potential, including the commonly used Navarro-Frenk-White, Hernquist and Plummer profiles.

Velocity anisotropy. Isotropic, constant-anisotropy, Osipkov-Merritt and
Cuddeford-Osipkov-Merritt models, the latter two radially (Type I) or tangentially (Type II) biased.

Distribution functions. Each anisotropy model’s distribution function, inverted from the
input density with exact symbolic expressions up to the final numerical integration, with
extensively validated numerical accuracy and checks that it is non-negative
(physical) and monotonic (dynamically stable).

Truncation in phase space. Model truncation performed in phase space, such that the
truncation boundary is fully self-consistent and in dynamical equilibrium, by two methods: one preserves the
model’s anisotropy profile (Method I), the other gives different anisotropy models an identical truncated
density (Method II).

Particles. Particle initial conditions with a finite, dynamically stable truncation
boundary, drawn from the truncated distribution function, in internal, model or physical units.

Observables. Radial, tangential and line-of-sight velocity dispersions,
line-of-sight velocity distributions and their Gauss-Hermite moments, and the local 3D velocity distribution at
any radius; projected quantities averaged over centered or offset circular and rectangular apertures.

Superposition. Distribution functions of different anisotropy models on one
truncated density, linearly superposed into one equilibrium model whose anisotropy profile lies beyond the
analytical families, such as one fitted to simulated halos.

Inference. End-to-end differentiable in JAX: the likelihood of a model against
kinematic data, and every observable, with gradients in the superposition weights, the unit scales and the
anisotropy parameters, for gradient-based Monte Carlo inference.


---

# Quick start

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/quickstart

# Quick start

The example of the first figure of Chiang+(2026d): an NFW halo with a constant velocity anisotropy of 0.25, truncated in
phase space at the virial mass of a concentration-10 halo, presented as a Milky Way-mass halo.

```
import pianistpy as pp
import astropy.units as u

# an untruncated NFW density profile with a constant velocity anisotropy of 0.25
halo = pp.Component(pp.DoublePowerLaw.nfw(), pp.Anisotropy(beta_c=0.25))

# the untruncated distribution function
df = pp.compute_df(halo)

# Method I: truncate it so that the truncated mass equals the virial mass of the
# untruncated NFW halo of concentration 10 (the mass inside 10 scale radii)
model = pp.truncate(df, pp.Truncation(mass_t=1.0, concentration=10))

# physical units: a halo of 1e12 solar masses with R_vir = c * r_0 = 200 kpc
model = model.to("physical", mass_0=1e12 * u.Msun, r_0=20 * u.kpc)

# draw ten million equal-mass particles centered at the origin and write them to a file
particles = pp.Sampler(model).sample(10_000_000, seed=1)
particles.write("NFW_Const0p25_Mt1e12_PARIC.h5")

# the line-of-sight velocity dispersion at three projected radii
sigma = pp.sigma_los(model, [2, 20, 100] * u.kpc)

```

pp.solve(halo, truncation) runs the two steps at once.

Every result carries a validation report with its accuracy tier, and a model is always a valid equilibrium; what
the package returns, flags and refuses is on one page, Flags and refusals.


---

# Representative computing time

Source: https://pianistpy.com/docs/start/timing

# Representative computing time

The table below times one chain of calls, from a density profile to the observables, built as in Chiang+(2026d): an isotropic NFW parent truncated by Method I, and a child at constant \(\beta_{\rm c} = 0.2\) built
from it by Method II. Each row is the median of three calls after one warm call, except row 6, the table’s
first build. The inputs are in internal units and every setting is at its default. The first two columns are one AMD Ryzen
Threadripper PRO 5975WX (64 threads, 256 GB, Linux), on its CPU alone and then with its NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Ti;
the third is an Intel Core Ultra 9 185H (22 threads, 32 GB, Windows 11), CPU only. These are trial runs on the
development tree; ver. 1.0.0 replaces them with runs on its own code.

Gray cells: the stage’s core runs on the CPU on every platform (the Poisson solve in rows 2 and 3, the table’s rows
in the worker pool in row 6), and the number is the stage’s wall-clock time with the GPU present. On the model, sigma_r and sigma_t each run the model’s
moments solve, and sigma_los and sigma_los_aperture each run that solve and the projection; nothing is kept
on the model between calls, so each row is the cost of one call. The aperture rows from the
table time a later call on the same aperture. The first call on a new aperture also finds the distribution
function’s extrema at the radii the table has not met, once per aperture, and the first aperture call on a table
starts its worker pool: on the Threadripper’s CPU the first call took 31.0 s.

On the Core Ultra 9 185H the table’s build (row 6) takes about five times the Threadripper’s wall-clock time. The rows
on the model run the moments solve serially on one core, and there the wall-clock time of identical calls differs by up to half
from one call to the next, so no ratio between the machines is given for them.
